Hypothesis: A spatially graded, *fixed-charge* defect landscape in a water-stable Zr6-oxo MOF—engineered as an anionically terminated outer shell (Zr–O–SO3− capped missing-linker sites) over a minimally defective, electronically benign core—will generate a measurable shell-to-core electrostatic potential (built-in field) that biases photogenerated carrier separation toward the catalytic surface and accelerates interfacial proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET). When a confined visible absorber is grown *only within a phase-confinement loading window* in the near-surface channel network (initially iodoplumbate MTP; contingency iodobismuthate/Cs3Bi2I9-like clusters), the combined architecture will (i) improve electron delivery to surface HER sites via band bending/potential gradient, (ii) increase HER kinetics via defect-local Zr–OH/Zr–OH2+ Brønsted acidity and optimized H* adsorption at defect-capped nodes (analogy to defect-driven CB/d-band tuning in photocatalytic MOFs), and (iii) suppress deleterious mobile-ion contributions to hysteresis by physically confining the absorber to sub-critical domain sizes and chemically tethering it at defect-capped sites—*provided* a pre-validated aqueous compatibility gate is met (no significant Pb/I leaching or I−/I3− photoredox runaway under the exact illumination/pH/ionic strength). The junction claim is rendered non-metaphorical by (a) specifying the fixed-charge chemistry (controlled fraction of Zr–O–SO3− vs neutral Zr–OH caps) and (b) pre-registering a falsifiable criterion: a reproducible shell-to-core contact potential difference ≥50–100 mV with correlated depth-dependent band-edge shifts by UPS/XPS; if this criterion is not met, the mechanism will be downgraded to ‘defect-site kinetics only’ and field-driven claims removed.
Plan:
Step 0 — System choice and quantitative design targets (set before synthesis)
0.1 MOF platform: select a Zr6-carboxylate with straight channels and known defect tolerance + aqueous stability. Primary: NU-1000 (Zr6 nodes, 1D mesoporous channels ~3 nm with microporous windows) to accommodate confined clusters while maintaining water stability; Alternative: UiO-67 derivative with enlarged apertures if NU-1000 chemistry proves incompatible with absorber precursors.
0.2 Defect-mode target: missing-linker defects only (node preserved). Acceptance bounds prior to absorber growth: (i) crystallinity retained (single-crystal or microcrystal PXRD peak broadening <15% vs parent), (ii) BET/Ar sorption pore volume loss <25%, (iii) no significant missing-cluster signatures in PDF/STEM (see Step 2).
0.3 Built-in field target: shell-to-core potential difference ≥50–100 mV across a 50–300 nm shell (measured on cross-sections), with matching depth-resolved band-edge/band-bending signatures.
0.4 Absorber phase-confinement target: absorber domain size (TEM/Scherrer) ≤ channel diameter and non-percolated (no continuous 3D MAPbI3-like domains). Define loading window as Pb (or Bi) wt% such that (i) PXRD lacks intense bulk perovskite reflections, (ii) STEM-EDX shows discontinuous domains confined to channels/shell region.

Step 1 — Grow low-defect starting crystals and pre-functionalize for controlled defect chemistry
1.1 Synthesize NU-1000 single crystals or large microcrystals via modulated solvothermal conditions (benzoic/formic acid modulators; low water activity), targeting low initial defect density (verified by digestion 1H NMR + TGA).
1.2 Introduce a minor fraction (5–15%) of linker functionality capable of later anchoring/capping chemistry without destabilizing Zr6 connectivity: (a) sulfonate-bearing dicarboxylate as *post-capable anion source* OR (b) pendant pyridyl groups to coordinate Pb/Bi without introducing strong acid in the same step. The mixed-linker choice is made to decouple “fixed negative charge” (via sulfonate capping) from “Brønsted acidity” (via controlled protonation of Zr–OH) so these variables can be independently tuned.
1.3 Activation: solvent exchange to ethanol/acetone and gentle activation (supercritical CO2 drying preferred) to avoid crack formation that would invalidate diffusion-limited shell control.

Step 2 — Create a core–shell missing-linker gradient while explicitly suppressing missing-cluster formation
2.1 Diffusion-limited, pulse-wise *linker exchange/etch* designed to favor missing-linker over node loss:
  - Etchant/capper: monocarboxylate buffer (acetate/formate) at low concentration (e.g., 5–50 mM) in DMF/EtOH with carefully limited water (≤1–2 vol% initially), operated in short pulses (e.g., 5–20 min) at 25–50 °C.
  - Rationale: mild monocarboxylates preferentially compete at Zr sites to displace a linker locally; catastrophic node removal is promoted by higher water activity/strong acid—both are minimized.
  - Shell thickness control: iterate pulses (e.g., 1–10 cycles), with quench/exchange into dry ethanol between pulses to stop defect propagation. Target 50–300 nm shell thickness via diffusion-limited kinetics; calibrate thickness vs cycle number using cross-sectional mapping (Step 3).
2.2 Immediate defect capping/repair to lock missing-linker modality:
  - Cap open Zr sites with either (a) neutral hydroxylation (Zr–OH/Zr–OH2+) by controlled water dosing or (b) anionic sulfonate termination by treatment with a sulfonate salt (e.g., R–SO3− Na+) under conditions that prevent framework hydrolysis.
  - Optional “node preservation” repair: brief exposure to the parent dicarboxylate linker at low concentration to re-ligate any incipient under-coordinated Zr sites (a controlled re-linking step). Proceed only if crystallinity is not compromised.
2.3 Defect-type discrimination (mandatory gate):
  - Total scattering/PDF: quantify Zr–Zr and Zr–O correlation changes characteristic of missing-cluster vs missing-linker.
  - High-resolution STEM on FIB lamellae: inspect node continuity and identify vacancy clusters.
  - Decision rule: if missing-cluster signatures exceed a predefined threshold (e.g., significant loss of node-node correlations in PDF and visible node voids in STEM), halt and adjust etch/cap conditions (lower water activity, shorter pulses, stronger immediate capping).

Step 3 — Operationally define and measure the built-in field (fixed-charge chemistry + potential mapping + band bending)
3.1 Define fixed-charge fraction: prepare a compositional series where the defect-rich shell has controlled Zr–O–SO3− coverage (e.g., 0%, 10%, 30%, 50% of defect sites anion-capped), while keeping the core largely neutral (predominantly Zr–OH capped).
3.2 Cross-section preparation: embed crystals in inert resin and prepare cross-sections by FIB milling to expose shell-to-core profiles without smearing surface chemistry.
3.3 Potential mapping:
  - Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) across the cross-section to extract contact potential difference (CPD) vs position; replicate across ≥10 crystals per condition.
  - Optional/confirmatory: off-axis electron holography (TEM) to map internal electrostatic potential in lamellae (where feasible).
3.4 Correlate potential with electronic structure:
  - Depth-resolved XPS/UPS (angle-resolved or sputter-free wedge geometry if available) to measure band-edge shifts and chemical state gradients (S 2p for sulfonate, O 1s for OH/H2O caps, Zr 3d).
  - Falsifiable criterion (pre-registered): accept “built-in field present” only if (i) KPFM shows ≥50–100 mV shell-to-core CPD and (ii) UPS/XPS reveals consistent depth-dependent band-edge shifts matching the CPD sign. Otherwise, proceed with the project but remove field-driven mechanistic attributions and treat defects as purely kinetic/chemical catalytic enhancers.

Step 4 — Aqueous compatibility and leaching/speciation gate (must pass before water splitting claims)
4.1 Define exact stress conditions matching intended photocatalysis: pH (buffered), ionic strength, dissolved O2 level, light flux/spectrum, temperature.
4.2 For iodoplumbate route (primary): quantify chemical stability independently of “ion migration”:
  - Time-resolved ICP-MS for Pb leaching under dark and illuminated conditions.
  - UV–vis to detect I3− formation (and iodide depletion) during illumination; track PbI2 signatures.
  - PXRD/PL before/after soaking and illumination to assess phase retention.
  - Pass/fail threshold (example): Pb leaching rate <1% of total Pb over 24 h under illumination; no net I3− accumulation beyond baseline; structural retention of MOF.
4.3 Contingency absorber (mandatory parallel track): implement a hydrolytically more robust visible absorber confined in the same channels and defect environment to decouple “migration” from “decomposition”:
  - Candidate: Cs3Bi2I9-like clusters/iodobismuthates (Sn-free) grown by sequential infiltration (BiI3 + CsI or organic ammonium iodide) with confinement control.
  - Apply the same leaching/speciation analytics (ICP-MS for Bi, UV–vis for polyiodides).
  - Decision logic: if iodoplumbate fails the gate, pivot to iodobismuthate for all photocatalysis mechanistic tests; retain iodoplumbate only for mechanistic comparison under non-aqueous or strictly protected conditions.

Step 5 — Quantitative phase-confinement model + explicit loading window to avoid 3D perovskite domains
5.1 Geometric confinement model:
  - Use channel diameter (from crystallography/sorption) to define maximum absorber crystallite size. For NU-1000 mesochannels (~3 nm), predict that 3D MAPbI3 (unit cell ~6.3 Å but requiring extended connectivity) will be disfavored beyond a few unit repeats; target 0D/1D iodoplumbate motifs or quasi-2D fragments terminated by bulky ammonium.
  - Define critical nucleus constraint: require that inferred domain sizes (Scherrer/TEM) remain ≤ channel diameter and that STEM-EDX shows no continuous percolation.
5.2 Kinetic control strategy beyond “dilute precursors”:
  - Sequential infiltration synthesis (SIS): (i) PbI2 infiltration at sub-saturation, (ii) rinse to remove external precursor, (iii) MAI/FAI vapor exposure at 40–70 °C for limited time, (iv) optional bulky ammonium iodide (e.g., phenethylammonium iodide) post-dose to terminate growth.
  - Explicit loading window study: vary Pb uptake in discrete steps (e.g., 0.1, 0.5, 1, 3, 5 wt% Pb) and map phase via GIWAXS/PXRD + TEM; identify the highest loading that still yields confined, non-percolated domains.
5.3 Distribution control relative to shell: exploit defect-capped shell binding (pyridyl/sulfonate) to bias nucleation toward near-surface channels; verify by cross-sectional STEM-EDX mapping (Pb/I or Bi/I gradients) and ToF-SIMS depth profiling.

Step 6 — Photocatalytic water splitting tests with mechanistic attribution tied to measured field, stability, and confinement
6.1 Stage-gated photocatalysis:
  - Stage A (screening): sacrificial donor HER under visible light; quantify apparent quantum yield; compare across fixed-charge series (0–50% sulfonate capping) and across absorber loading window.
  - Stage B (overall splitting): only after passing aqueous compatibility gate; integrate OER partner/cocatalyst as needed.
6.2 Co-catalyst placement: photodeposit Pt or deposit earth-abundant cocatalyst (Ni2P/MoSx) with preference for defect-rich shell; verify spatial localization by cross-sectional EDX.
6.3 Mechanistic measurements aligned to reviewer directives:
  - Correlate HER rate with (i) measured CPD (KPFM) and (ii) depth-resolved band-edge shifts (UPS/XPS) to test field-driven separation.
  - Transient absorption / time-resolved PL to extract carrier lifetime changes vs CPD magnitude.
  - PCET/proton handling: quantify surface acidity (pyridine-IR or NH3-TPD analog where feasible; titration of Brønsted sites) and relate to HER kinetics.
6.4 Ion migration vs decomposition discrimination:
  - If iodoplumbate is used: impedance spectroscopy under dark/light and humidity control; bias-stress hysteresis in photocurrent/PL; ToF-SIMS after soaking/illumination to detect iodide redistribution *only after* confirming minimal leaching.
  - Compare against iodobismuthate analog (expected lower mobile-ion artifacts) to separate migration effects from chemical instability.

Step 7 — Stability and integrity (operando + post-mortem)
7.1 Operando PXRD and UV–vis during photocatalysis to confirm phase persistence.
7.2 ICP-MS tracking (Pb/Bi and Zr) during cycling; predefined acceptable Zr leaching limits.
7.3 Post-mortem microscopy (FIB-STEM) to verify that (i) shell gradient persists, (ii) absorber remains confined, and (iii) no macroscopic cracking/porosity collapse occurred.

Deliverables (explicit acceptance milestones)
M1: Verified missing-linker-dominant shell gradient with preserved node lattice (PDF/STEM) and retained porosity.
M2: Verified fixed-charge gradient and measurable CPD ≥50–100 mV with matched UPS/XPS depth band shifts.
M3: Demonstrated aqueous compatibility gate pass (or pivot to iodobismuthate).
M4: Demonstrated confined absorber within defined loading window (no 3D percolation).
M5: Photocatalytic HER enhancement that correlates quantitatively with CPD and defect chemistry, not merely with absorber loading.
Feasibility:
Addresses (i) “junction/field” rigor: The proposal no longer treats the built-in field as an analogy. Fixed charge is chemically instantiated by a controlled fraction of anionic sulfonate termination (Zr–O–SO3−) versus neutral hydroxyl caps, and the potential profile is measured directly on cross-sections (KPFM; optional electron holography) with a pre-registered falsifiable threshold (≥50–100 mV) and corroborated by depth-resolved UPS/XPS band-edge shifts. If the threshold is not met, the field-driven mechanism is explicitly rejected and the work proceeds under a kinetics-only framework.

Addresses (ii) iodoplumbate + acidity + water incompatibility: The plan inserts a decisive stability/speciation gate *before* water-splitting claims, using time-resolved ICP-MS for Pb, UV–vis for I3−, and operando structural probes under the exact photocatalytic pH/ionic strength/light flux. A mandatory contingency absorber (Sn-free iodobismuthate/Cs3Bi2I9-like clusters) is integrated to decouple “ion migration” phenomena from outright chemical decomposition/leaching; this ensures the core architecture (defect-gradient + confinement + potential mapping) remains testable even if iodoplumbates fail in aqueous acidic microenvironments.

Addresses (iii) defect modality control: The etch strategy is redesigned to minimize missing-cluster formation (low water activity, mild monocarboxylate pulses, immediate capping/repair). Missing-linker vs missing-cluster is not assumed; it is discriminated by total scattering/PDF and HR-STEM on FIB lamellae with explicit acceptance bounds on crystallinity and porosity before proceeding to absorber growth.

Addresses (iv) confinement/phase control quantitatively: A channel-size–bounded phase-confinement model is tied to explicit, experimentally enforced loading windows (Pb/Bi wt% series) and domain-size constraints verified by Scherrer/TEM and cross-sectional STEM-EDX/ToF-SIMS. Growth is controlled kinetically through sequential infiltration plus growth-terminating bulky ammonium iodides rather than relying on dilution alone. This makes the causal chain between confinement, non-percolated domains, reduced mobile-ion artifacts, and improved photocatalysis testable.

Link to established empirical logic: Prior demonstrations that semiconductor/MOF confinement improves charge separation and stability (e.g., QD@MOF water splitting) support the composite strategy, while defect engineering in MOFs is known to tune adsorption energetics and suppress recombination, motivating the defect-capped catalytic shell. The present proposal advances these ideas by adding (a) spatial defect gradients with verified defect modality, and (b) direct, quantitative mapping of electrostatic potential and band bending as the mechanistic linchpin rather than an inferred effect.
Critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-pre-registered proposal with clear mechanistic checkpoints, explicit falsification criteria, and strong separation of variables (defect modality vs fixed charge vs acidity vs absorber stability). Engineering resolution is high due to concrete diffusion-limited defect protocols, cross-sectional potential mapping, and mandatory gating steps. Logical consistency is strong: the built-in field claim is chemically instantiated and experimentally verifiable, with a predefined downgrade path if unmet. Minor weaknesses arise from cumulative complexity and risk: the simultaneous control of defect gradients, sulfonate coverage, absorber confinement, and aqueous stability may stretch experimental bandwidth, and the assumed magnitude of achievable CPD (50–100 mV) in hydrated MOFs remains ambitious even with fixed charges. Evidence grounding is solid and largely disciplined, though some analogies to band bending/d-band tuning in inorganic photocatalysts may not fully translate to MOF electronic structures. The rationale is creative and addresses a real bottleneck (non-metaphorical junctions in MOFs), but it partially relies on the success of iodometalate confinement strategies that are still emerging and system-sensitive.

Hypothesis: A cationic Ni(II) MOF built from a deliberately *controllably labile* dinuclear Ni2(μ2-OH)(carboxylate)3(pyridyl)2 SBU will achieve higher oxoanion sorption capacity (qmax) and faster uptake kinetics (reduced t90) when activated by a crystallography-guided *partial* desolvation protocol that generates a quantified fraction of open/weakly ligated axial Ni sites while retaining accessible pore connectivity. The mechanistic claim is explicitly falsifiable: (i) partial desolvation creates an “open-site population” (axial vacancy fraction, fvac) that increases the intrinsic anion-exchange rate constant (kex) via transient inner-sphere coordination to Ni and cooperative outer-sphere H-bonding to μ2-OH; (ii) any desolvation-induced unit-cell contraction can either increase or decrease intracrystalline mobility depending on whether the *accessible pore volume and pore limiting diameter* (PLD) are preserved—therefore transport acceleration is predicted only within an activation window defined by simultaneously high fvac and non-degraded connectivity metrics (PLD/accessible volume from zeo++/PLATON); and (iii) the observed rate enhancement will be attributable to a shift in the rate-determining step only if independently measured mobility (ionic conductivity/PFG-NMR tracer diffusion) increases and the uptake activation energy decreases in the partially desolvated state. This refined framework avoids overclaiming “electrostatic potential gradients” and instead ties contraction/desolvation to measurable structure descriptors (fvac, PLD, accessible pore volume) and independent mobility/activation-energy observables, while explicitly stress-testing the under-coordinated Ni/μ2-OH node against aquation, hydrolysis, and Ni leaching across pH 4–9 and competitive anion backgrounds.
Plan:
Step 1 — Resolve SBU stoichiometry/charge balance and engineer controlled lability (pre-registered chemistry).
1.1. Target node and charge accounting (explicit): synthesize a cationic framework containing Ni2(μ2-OH)(O2CR)3(Lpy)2 cores where (a) three carboxylates are bridging (net −3), μ2-OH contributes −1, and Ni2 contributes +4; the resulting SBU core is charge-neutral before axial ligation, while *framework cationicity* is introduced by using a net-cationic linker set (e.g., incorporating a quaternized pyridinium-bearing ditopic linker as a fraction of Lpy) or by embedding cationic pendant groups on the linker backbone. Counteranions (SO4^2−/HSO4−) are incorporated in channels during synthesis for ion exchange.
1.2. Design for lability without catastrophic undercoordination: enforce a square-pyramidal/octahedral Ni environment in the as-synthesized state with axial positions occupied by labile neutral ligands (H2O/MeOH/DMF), and tune axial lability by (i) selecting pyridyl donors that are less labile than solvent yet do not occupy both axial sites, and (ii) sterically biasing one axial site to be weakly bound (longer Ni–Osolv) as determined by SCXRD.
1.3. Phase generation: prepare (i) mm-scale single crystals for SC–SC tracking and (ii) microcrystalline fractions with narrow particle-size cuts (e.g., 0.5–1 μm; 2–5 μm; 10–20 μm by controlled synthesis/sieving) for kinetic discrimination.
1.4. Baseline characterization (pre-activation): SCXRD (node geometry, solvent occupancy, counterion location/occupancy), PXRD (phase purity), ICP-OES/MS (Ni content), CHNS/combustion, TGA-EGA (solvent identity/amount), and FT-IR.

Step 2 — Crystallography-guided partial desolvation activation (CG-PDA) with quantitative structural descriptors (mandatory directive #4).
2.1. SCXRD-derived pore/connectivity metrics: from each refined SCXRD model compute pore limiting diameter (PLD), largest cavity diameter (LCD), accessible surface area, and accessible pore volume using zeo++ (probe radii pre-registered: 1.4 Å for H2O; 2.0–2.4 Å to bracket oxoanion effective sizes) and cross-check with PLATON SQUEEZE/VOID analyses.
2.2. Humidity-programmed activation: use DVS-controlled a_w steps (e.g., 0.95 → 0.75 → 0.50 → 0.30 → 0.20) at fixed temperature (e.g., 298 K) with equilibration criteria defined by mass change rate (<0.01% min−1 over 30 min). Collect in situ variable-humidity PXRD to track unit-cell parameters.
2.3. SC–SC tracking with fragility mitigation: limit SCXRD to a pre-registered maximum of 3–4 states per single crystal (as-synthesized; two intermediate a_w points; final chosen activation state) and replicate across ≥5 crystals; implement low-dose data collection, crystal mounting that maintains humidity (capillary with mother liquor vapor), and mosaicity/twinning checks.
2.4. Define activation window by quantitative, dual descriptors:
  • Structural window: fvac (fraction of Ni axial sites vacated from SCXRD occupancies + EXAFS coordination numbers) ≥ 0.25 while PLD and accessible pore volume remain ≥ 90% of the solvated state (zeo++).
  • Stability window: Ni loss during water exposure/uptake test ≤ 0.5% of total Ni per cycle (ICP of supernatant) and ligand loss below LOQ by LC-UV/LC-MS.
Only states satisfying both are advanced to full sorption/kinetics campaigns.

Step 3 — Independent transport/mobility quantification vs structural contraction (mandatory directive #1; replaces “electrostatic gradient” claim).
3.1. Ionic mobility metric A (preferred): electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) on oriented single-crystal aggregates or pressed pellets with controlled orientation if feasible.
  • Prepare oriented beds (align 1D channel axis via mild magnetic alignment if crystals are anisotropic, or by sedimentation alignment on patterned substrates).
  • Measure ionic conductivity in aqueous electrolyte (background ionic strength fixed) for solvated vs partially desolvated vs fully desolvated states, extracting bulk resistance and activation energies from temperature-dependent EIS (e.g., 288–318 K).
3.2. Ionic mobility metric B (if feasible): PFG-NMR tracer diffusion using a suitable NMR-active oxoanion analog (e.g., 19F-containing tracer such as BF4−/PF6− for cationic channel environments, or 77Se for selenate where instrument access allows). Report Dtracer with error bars; compare across activation states.
3.3. Temperature-dependent uptake: perform uptake kinetics at ≥3 temperatures (e.g., 288/298/308 K) and extract apparent activation energies (Eapp) under conditions where film transport is minimized (see Step 4). A decrease in Eapp concurrent with increased mobility supports the transport-acceleration claim; an increase indicates pore constriction dominates.

Step 4 — Falsifiable, hierarchical kinetics mechanism package (mandatory directive #2).
4.1. Experimental design for discriminating limitations:
  • Particle-size series: run identical uptake experiments on at least three size fractions (0.5–1 μm; 2–5 μm; 10–20 μm). Intracrystalline diffusion control predicts characteristic time ∝ L^2; exchange-limited predicts weak size dependence.
  • Stirring-rate series: vary external mass transfer (e.g., 200/600/1000 rpm) at constant particle size to test film diffusion; film-limited rates scale with stirring.
  • Concentration series: vary initial oxoanion concentration to probe site-limited saturation and rate dependence.
4.2. Single-crystal uptake imaging (spatiotemporal):
  • Use μXRF/EDS line scans (and/or confocal Raman mapping if anion has signature bands) along the crystallographic channel axis during partial uptake times to detect diffusion fronts/gradients.
  • Fit concentration profiles to 1D diffusion-reaction models to extract Deff and kex with confidence intervals.
4.3. Model hierarchy and selection (pre-registered): fit datasets to a nested set of mechanistic models rather than generic pseudo-order fits:
  • M1: external film diffusion + instantaneous sorption (mass-transfer coefficient kf).
  • M2: intraparticle diffusion in 1D channels (Deff) with boundary film term.
  • M3: diffusion + finite exchange reaction at sites (Deff + kex).
  • M4: dual-population sites (open Ni sites + noncoordinating ion-exchange sites) with distinct kex values and capacities.
Select models by AIC/BIC with bootstrapped confidence intervals; report parameter identifiability (profile likelihood) and goodness-of-fit to both time traces and spatial profiles.

Step 5 — Sorption capacity/selectivity tied to structural state.
5.1. Oxoanion targets: SeO4^2− and HAsO4^2−/H2AsO4− with pH-controlled speciation; optional ReO4− as a monovalent geometric analog to decouple charge effects.
5.2. Isotherms: collect equilibrium isotherms for each activation state at fixed ionic strength (e.g., 1–10 mM background electrolyte) and specified pH (e.g., 6.5–7.5 for environmentally relevant). Fit with Langmuir/Freundlich *only as descriptive*, while mechanistic interpretation uses site counts from SCXRD/EXAFS.
5.3. Competition: test Cl−, NO3−, HCO3−, SO4^2−, PO4^3− at environmentally relevant ratios; quantify selectivity coefficients and capacity retention.

Step 6 — Mechanism-specific structural validation (binding mode + node integrity).
6.1. Guest-validated structures: SCXRD (where feasible) of loaded crystals from within activation window to identify inner-sphere Ni–O(oxoanion) binding versus outer-sphere μ2-OH hydrogen bonding; quantify occupancies and disorder.
6.2. XAS/EXAFS operando and post-mortem: Ni K-edge XANES/EXAFS on (i) solvated, (ii) partially desolvated, (iii) loaded, and (iv) cycled samples to quantify Ni coordination number changes and rule out conversion to Ni(OH)2/NiOOH signatures.
6.3. Leaching/ligand release package (mandatory directive #3):
  • Operando Ni leaching: ICP-OES/MS of supernatants vs time during uptake at pH 4, 6.5, 9 and with competitors.
  • Ligand release: LC-UV/LC-MS quantification of linker fragments in supernatants.
  • Acceptance criterion: within the activation window, cumulative Ni loss ≤0.5% per cycle and no increasing trend over ≥10 cycles.

Step 7 — Controls to establish causality.
7.1. Control A (non-labile Ni): isoreticular Ni MOF with saturated axial positions (e.g., strongly bound axial ligands or a node topology that lacks accessible axial sites) to isolate the effect of open-site creation.
7.2. Control B (no μ2-OH): same topology but μ2-O replaced/absent (synthetic analog), isolating H-bond relay contribution to capacity/kinetics.
7.3. Control C (contraction without open sites, if accessible): a framework that contracts under desolvation but maintains fully coordinated Ni, to decouple contraction effects from site creation.

Pre-registered success/failure outcomes (falsifiable).
• Success requires simultaneous: (i) partially desolvated state shows increased mobility (higher conductivity or higher Dtracer) and lower Eapp than solvated state; (ii) kinetics show size-scaling consistent with increased Deff and/or increased kex depending on state; (iii) qmax increases relative to fully desolvated (accessibility restored) without unacceptable Ni/ligand loss.
• Failure modes are informative: if contraction reduces PLD/accessible volume and mobility drops, uptake slows—this directly falsifies any universal “contraction accelerates transport” narrative and will redirect to linker/SBU redesign to maintain PLD while creating fvac.
Feasibility:
1) Literature-anchored rationale with tightened claims: High-capacity oxoanion capture by cationic Ni(II) MOFs via ion exchange is validated (Asset 1), but this proposal adds a quantitative, state-resolved activation variable rather than assuming activation is benign. SBU geometry controlling sorption behavior is well-established (Asset 2), and SC–SC, desolvation-linked kinetic acceleration via channel transport is plausible (Asset 4) but here is reframed into measurable pore/connectivity and mobility metrics (zeo++/PLATON + EIS/PFG-NMR + temperature-dependent kinetics), directly addressing reviewer concern (i).
2) Node stoichiometry and aqueous stability are treated as first-class risk items: charge balance is explicitly engineered (counteranions in channels; framework cationicity via linker design), and the under-coordinated/open-site concept is constrained to an activation window bounded by quantified Ni/ligand leaching thresholds across pH 4–9 and competitors, with EXAFS to rule out Ni hydroxide/oxyhydroxide formation (addresses concern (ii) and mandatory directive #3).
3) Kinetics are made diagnostic and falsifiable: instead of relying on pseudo-order fits, the plan pre-registers discriminating experiments (particle size, stirring rate, temperature dependence, single-crystal spatial profiling) and a hierarchical diffusion–reaction model selection workflow with confidence intervals and identifiability checks (addresses concern (iii) and mandatory directive #2).
4) SCXRD fragility is mitigated and de-risked: the SC–SC program limits the number of humidity states per crystal, uses replication, and moves the activation-window definition away from PXRD peak width to quantitative structural (fvac, PLD, accessible volume) and stability (Ni loss per cycle) descriptors tied to function, satisfying mandatory directive #4 and addressing concern (iv). Even if some crystals fail, the microcrystalline kinetics/mobility and post-mortem structural probes still deliver the mechanistic package.
5) Clear decision points: The proposal is structured with go/no-go criteria (activation window thresholds, mobility increase requirement, leaching limits). This ensures that if partial desolvation constricts pores or destabilizes Ni nodes, the mechanism is rejected early and the design is iterated (e.g., linker sterics to preserve PLD, alternative counteranions, or reduced open-site fraction) rather than forcing an overconfident narrative.
Critique: The proposal is unusually rigorous and falsifiable, with good separation of structural, transport, and reactivity contributions. The strongest elements are (i) pre-registered activation-window criteria linking fvac and connectivity to function, (ii) hierarchical diffusion–reaction model selection with identifiability checks, and (iii) explicit stability/leaching acceptance criteria across pH and competitors. Score deductions are driven by several technical risks and some under-specified feasibility points: (1) Quantifying fvac by SCXRD solvent occupancies is intrinsically fragile—partial occupancy of disordered axial solvent and counterions can be highly model-dependent, and EXAFS coordination numbers may not uniquely resolve “vacancy” versus substitution by anions/water during handling; the plan needs tighter operando control to prevent rehydration artifacts. (2) The EIS plan is ambitious for MOF powders/pellets in aqueous electrolyte; separating true intracrystalline ion mobility from interparticle/contact resistances and electrode polarization is nontrivial, and “oriented aggregates” is not yet a concrete, proven method in this context. (3) PFG-NMR tracer diffusion choices (BF4−/PF6−) may be chemically incompatible with a strongly anion-exchanging, water-exposed cationic Ni MOF (competitive binding, hydrolysis, or poor relevance to oxoanions); 77Se is elegant but may be impractical. (4) The proposed control B (no μ2-OH) may be synthetically unrealistic while preserving topology and Ni2 node identity; similarly, control C (contraction without open sites) may be difficult to realize without changing many confounders. (5) The core synthetic premise—creating framework cationicity via a “fraction of quaternized pyridinium-bearing ditopic linker” while retaining crystallinity/SC–SC behavior and stable Ni2(μ2-OH) nodes—may be the dominant risk and is not yet supported by a contingency plan (e.g., post-synthetic quaternization vs mixed-linker solvothermal routes vs cationic metalloligands).

Hypothesis: Zn‑PYI1 can be transformed into a crystallinity‑retaining, permanently porous metalloenzyme‑mimetic by a two-layer catalytic architecture that explicitly de-risks Zn‑carboxylate fragility: (i) a topotactic, low‑fraction solvent‑assisted linker exchange (SALE) installs a latent, inward-facing carbonyl handle on an isoreticular PYI strut while preserving the primary organocatalyst geometry enforced by the Zn-carboxylate lattice; (ii) a water-activity–controlled dynamic covalent manifold (preferentially oxime/hydrazone; imine as a secondary route) programs an adaptive second-sphere microenvironment (H-bonding + Brønsted acid/base + polarity) around the fixed PYI site. Mechanistically, the lattice provides a rigid first-sphere “active-site frame” (crystallinity) that fixes the relative positioning of photoredox (triphenylamine) and organocatalyst (PYI) motifs, while the reversible C=N chemistry acts as an error-correcting, self-healing second sphere that can (a) pre-organize aldehyde/enamine formation, (b) electrostatically and H-bond stabilize the enamine–radical-cation coupled transition state in photoinduced asymmetric α-alkylation, and (c) suppress nonselective solution pathways by increasing internal effective molarity and restricting radical diffusion/recombination. The refined approach overcomes the reviewers’ chemistry–structure interface concerns by (1) avoiding strong aqueous acid for deprotection (switch to MOF-compatible carbonyl unmasking and/or direct carbonyl-linker exchange), (2) operating under quantified low water activity (Karl Fischer–verified solvents; molecular sieves; buffered catalysts), and (3) replacing unquantified “self-sorting” with a measurable selectivity hierarchy (competitive uptake/isotherms + in-pore speciation by ssNMR/XPS) that predicts which amines occupy which fraction of carbonyl sites as a function of pKa, size, and diffusion. Catalytic gains are predicted to correlate with a defined pocket-density parameter (ρpocket = xexchange × θC=N loading) and with site-isolation metrics proving pore-internal turnover dominates over external surface catalysis.
Plan:
Step 0 — Define quantitative go/no-go gates (mandatory derisking milestones)
0.1. Crystallinity gate (all postsynthetic steps): PXRD similarity index ≥ 0.90 vs parent (peak positions within ±0.05° 2θ; no new dominant phases), and (where crystals permit) unit-cell volume change |ΔV| ≤ 3% by SCXRD or Le Bail refinement.
0.2. Permanent porosity gate: BET surface area retention ≥ 70% of parent Zn‑PYI1 after each critical step (post-SALE; post-carbonyl unmasking; post-pocket installation), and micropore volume retention ≥ 65% (NLDFT).
0.3. Chemical stability gate: Zn leaching during any treatment or catalysis ≤ 1.0 wt% of total Zn per cycle (ICP‑MS of supernatants), and carboxylate-linker loss/defect increase limited to ≤ 5% relative change by quantitative digest NMR mass balance (total linker:Zn ratio) plus TGA consistency.
0.4. Internal-site catalysis gate: (i) external poisoning reduces activity ≤ 20% (internal remains), while (ii) pore blocking reduces activity ≥ 60% (internal required), and (iii) initial rate shows weak particle-size dependence consistent with internal diffusion control only beyond a defined size regime (see Step 3.4).

Step 1 — Baseline reproduction and controls (structure–function anchor)
1.1. Synthesize Zn‑PYI1 and activate under literature-consistent conditions; prepare three particle-size cuts (e.g., ~0.5–1 µm, 2–5 µm, 20–50 µm) by controlled crystallization/sonication/sieving; measure size distributions (SEM + laser diffraction).
1.2. Baseline characterization: PXRD, N2/Ar sorption (BET, NLDFT), CO2 (273 K) for ultramicropore access, TGA, and photocatalytic asymmetric α‑alkylation benchmarking under fixed photon flux (actinometry), fixed stirring, identical catalyst mass and optical path. Record: initial rates, yields, ee, quantum yield (apparent), and recyclability (≥5 cycles).
1.3. Establish homogeneous and “physical mixture” controls: (i) homogeneous PYI organocatalyst + triphenylamine analogue (if available) + amine additives; (ii) physical mixture of parent Zn‑PYI1 with the same amine additives not tethered; these define the non-confinement baseline.

Step 2 — Linker editing with explicit SCSC derisking (SALE fraction control)
2.1. Linker design options (choose primary + contingency):
  - Primary path A (avoid post-exchange acid deprotection): synthesize an isoreticular PYI-derived dicarboxylate linker bearing a directly accessible aldehyde (L‑CHO) but electronically deactivated toward side reactions (e.g., aromatic aldehyde separated by a short alkyl spacer to reduce coordination interference) and lacking extra donor atoms.
  - Contingency path B (latent carbonyl, MOF-compatible unmasking): synthesize L‑Acetal (acetal-protected aldehyde) OR L‑Diol precursor that can be oxidized in-pore to aldehyde under neutral conditions (e.g., TEMPO/bleach-type oxidations are excluded; instead use mild, non-aqueous oxidants compatible with Zn-carboxylates; final selection determined by stability screen in Step 2.5).
  - Nonreactive control linker L‑Me (steric/electronic analog lacking carbonyl reactivity).
2.2. SALE protocol (topotactic constraints): perform SALE on activated Zn‑PYI1 in non-coordinating solvent (e.g., chlorinated solvent/alkane + minimal polar co-solvent as required for linker solubility; exclude DMF/strong amide donors if they increase lability) at 40–70 °C with low linker concentration to minimize dissolution–reprecipitation. Target xexchange = 0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20.
2.3. Time-course sampling to prove topotaxy: collect aliquots at multiple time points; quantify exchange fraction by digest 1H NMR (integral ratios of native vs introduced linker), and verify crystallinity retention by high-resolution PXRD; accept only conditions meeting gates 0.1–0.3.
2.4. Defect quantification and lattice lability check: (i) total scattering/PDF before/after SALE to detect local Zn–O distortions; (ii) thermogravimetry/digest NMR for linker:Zn stoichiometry; (iii) quantify any increase in missing-linker defects indirectly via increased uptake of a defect-probe (e.g., small polar probe gas vs parent) while ensuring micropore retention.
2.5. Carbonyl-handle viability screen (small-scale stability matrix): expose SALE materials to candidate unmasking/activation conditions in sealed vials with controlled water activity (aw) and quantify: PXRD similarity, BET retention, and Zn leaching. Only one protocol is promoted to full workflow:
  - Validated protocol requirement: demonstrate ≥70% BET retention and ≤1 wt% Zn loss after 24 h treatment.

Step 2b — Carbonyl activation/unmasking with water-activity control (explicit protocol + contingency)
2b.1. If direct L‑CHO is used: skip deprotection and proceed to pocket formation.
2b.2. If acetal deprotection is required (contingency, only if Step 2.5 passes): perform acetal hydrolysis under strictly controlled low aw using anhydrous alcohol solvent pre-dried to <200 ppm H2O (Karl Fischer), 3Å molecular sieves, and catalytic, non-coordinating Brønsted acid at minimal loading (screen: 0.1–1 mol% relative to acetal sites). Keep crystals solvent-filled at all times; avoid vacuum drying until after neutralization and thorough solvent exchange.
2b.3. If any deprotection condition violates gates: pivot to oxime/hydrazone strategy using a carbonyl that does not require acid (direct L‑CHO), or pivot to in-pore formation of oxime/hydrazone from a ketone handle that is installed directly.

Step 3 — Pocket programming with quantified “assembly rules” (replace qualitative self-sorting)
3.1. Choose dynamic covalent bond type based on stability matrix:
  - Preferred: oxime or hydrazone formation (greater hydrolytic stability than imines; still reversible under mild conditions), using aminooxy or hydrazide residues as second-sphere “modules”.
  - Secondary: imines only if Step 2.5 shows stability under required aw and pH window.
3.2. Define pocket-density parameter and loading control:
  - ρpocket = xexchange × θC=N, where θC=N is fractional conversion of carbonyl sites to C=N adduct (quantified by digest NMR and ssNMR integration).
  - Target θC=N levels: 0.25, 0.50, 0.75 at each xexchange to decouple “how many handles” from “how fully occupied”.
3.3. Quantify competitive uptake/selectivity (mandatory):
  - Measure single-component uptake isotherms in solvent (or vapor, if feasible) for each amine/aminooxy module to obtain apparent partition coefficients (Kpore).
  - Perform competitive uptake experiments (binary/ternary mixtures) and determine selectivity factors Sij = (qi/qj)pore / (Ci/Cj)solution. Use these Sij values to design mixtures that predictably enrich a desired module near the carbonyl handles.
3.4. Replace “self-sorting triad” with rule-based assembly:
  - Construct a minimal “His-like” module (aminoimidazole derivative via C=N chemistry), an “Asp/Glu-like” anionic/polar module (carboxylate/sulfonate-bearing aminooxy/hydrazide), and a “Ser-like” H-bond donor module (aminoalcohol aminooxy/hydrazide).
  - Assembly strategy A (sequential with equilibrium reset): install module 1 to partial θ, wash/exchange, then module 2, then module 3; leverage reversibility by applying a mild catalyst (buffered) to allow error correction, followed by solvent exchange to freeze composition.
  - Assembly strategy B (competitive mixture with predicted outcome): use the measured Sij and diffusion/size data to set feed ratios that target a specified internal composition (e.g., 1:1:1 occupancy within ±10%).
  - Heterogeneity assessment (mandatory): ssNMR (13C/15N CP/MAS) lineshape/broadening analysis to estimate distribution of C=N environments; corroborate with XPS N 1s deconvolution and, where possible, spatial mapping (e.g., micro-FTIR mapping across single crystals) to rule out shell-only functionalization.
3.5. Optional locking step (only after best dynamic pocket identified): reduce C=N adducts to secondary amines under rigorously screened mild conditions (small-scale first), ensuring gates 0.1–0.3 remain satisfied. Maintain an unreduced series to compare “dynamic vs static” function.

Step 4 — Internal-site proof: discriminate pore vs external surface catalysis (mandatory)
4.1. External-site selective poisoning: graft/block external surface with a bulky, non-penetrating reagent that binds/quenches accessible basic sites (size-excluded from pores), then test catalytic activity. Pass criterion: ≤20% loss vs unpoisoned sample.
4.2. Pore-blocking experiment: introduce a bulky, pore-occupying but catalytically inert guest that is known to enter the channels and reduce free volume (quantify by sorption decrease). Pass criterion: ≥60% loss in initial rate and/or ee collapse consistent with loss of confinement.
4.3. Particle-size dependence: compare initial rates and ee across size cuts at identical loading and photon flux. Internal catalysis expectation: (i) rates decrease with increasing crystal size if diffusion-limited; (ii) if external sites dominated, rates scale with external area and show stronger size dependence even when pores are blocked. Use these trends with Thiele-modulus-style interpretation to support internal turnover.
4.4. Leaching/homogeneous contribution test: hot filtration (or light-off filtration) and continuation of reaction in filtrate; require ≤5% additional conversion in filtrate over matched time.

Step 5 — Structure–function correlations tied to quantitative descriptors (address reviewer request)
5.1. Correlate catalytic metrics (kobs, yield, ee, apparent quantum yield) against: xexchange, θC=N, ρpocket, BET/micropore volume, diffusion proxy (uptake kinetics), and heterogeneity metrics (ssNMR linewidth/peak ratios).
5.2. Mechanism probes with decision outcomes:
  - Water/protic additive sensitivity mapped vs dynamic bond type (oxime/hydrazone vs imine) to verify that performance changes track C=N equilibrium rather than framework degradation.
  - H-bond/acid–base perturbation: add competitive H-bond acceptors/donors; quantify changes in ee/rate to infer second-sphere involvement.
  - Photophysics: transient absorption/EPR (if available) to compare radical lifetimes/back-electron transfer rates vs ρpocket; link improved ee to altered radical persistence within pores.
5.3. Confinement beyond size-selectivity: site-isolation metric by comparing turnover frequency normalized to internal functional loading (from digest NMR) and showing super-linear dependence of ee (or rate) on ρpocket consistent with cooperative pocket effects rather than additive external catalysis.

Step 6 — Stability, recyclability, and self-healing demonstration
6.1. Multi-cycle tests (≥8 cycles) with PXRD + sorption after cycles 1, 3, 5, 8; enforce gates 0.1–0.3.
6.2. Compare dynamic vs locked pockets: dynamic materials should show partial recovery of activity/ee after deliberate perturbation (e.g., brief exposure to competitive binder then removal), whereas locked pockets should not—directly testing “enzyme-like adaptivity”.
Feasibility:
This revision directly addresses the reviewers’ three feasibility risks with explicit quantitative milestones and contingency chemistry.

(1) Framework survivability through carbonyl unmasking and C=N chemistry: The plan no longer depends on repeated aqueous/acidic treatments as a default. The primary route installs an already-unmasked aldehyde (L‑CHO) via low-fraction SALE to minimize lattice stress. If protection is unavoidable, unmasking is screened in a water-activity–controlled matrix (Karl Fischer thresholds; molecular sieves; minimal acid) with pass/fail gates for PXRD similarity (≥0.90), BET retention (≥70%), and Zn leaching (≤1 wt%). This gatekeeping converts “SCSC asserted” into a decision-controlled workflow that stops before irreversible damage.

(2) Water/acid management vs permanent porosity: Dynamic covalent assembly is shifted to oxime/hydrazone as the preferred manifold because it is generally more hydrolytically robust than imines while still reversible enough for error-correction; imines are retained as a secondary option only if stability gates are met. Permanent porosity is protected by keeping pores solvent-filled during transformations, using gentle activation (e.g., scCO2 when needed), and requiring micropore volume retention ≥65% after each critical step.

(3) Pocket assembly rules and heterogeneity control: “Self-sorting” is replaced with measurable selectivity factors (competitive uptake/isotherms) and a defined pocket-density descriptor (ρpocket = xexchange × θC=N). Heterogeneity is not assumed away: ssNMR lineshape analysis + XPS speciation + (where feasible) spatially resolved vibrational mapping are specified to detect shell-only functionalization or broad distributions of C=N environments. These measurements feed back into assembly strategy (sequential vs competitive) and into catalysis correlations.

Internal-site proof and confinement controls are upgraded beyond size-selectivity: a paired external-poisoning vs pore-blocking logic with explicit pass thresholds, particle-size dependence across three size cuts, and leaching/hot-filtration criteria together establish whether turnover occurs predominantly within pores. Finally, structure–function correlation is enforced by mapping rate/ee vs (xexchange, θC=N, ρpocket, diffusion proxies, and heterogeneity metrics), enabling a reviewer-satisfying link between pocket geometry/spacing and catalytic outcomes.

This derisking logic is consistent with prior demonstrations that (i) multivariate postsynthetic modifications can preserve crystallinity/porosity when reactions are chosen to match framework stability windows (Assets 1–2), and (ii) Zn‑PYI MOFs deliver synergistic catalysis when cooperative functions are integrated rather than physically mixed (Asset 3). The revised plan adopts the same integration principle while adding conservative stability gates and fallback chemistries to keep Zn‑carboxylate integrity central rather than assumed.
Critique: Methodologically, the proposal is unusually well-engineered for Zn‑carboxylate fragility: it defines hard go/no-go gates (PXRD similarity, BET/micropore retention, Zn leaching, defect mass balance) and includes credible internal-site validation (paired external poisoning/pore blocking, size cuts, hot filtration). The main scientific risk is that the central mechanistic claim—second-sphere modules stabilizing an enamine–radical-cation coupled transition state and suppressing radical diffusion/recombination—remains under-specified in terms of measurable, discriminating observables. Several proposed probes (ssNMR/XPS lineshapes, uptake selectivities) establish composition and heterogeneity, but they do not directly verify the hypothesized H-bond/electrostatic organization at the reactive intermediate stage. Additionally, topotactic SALE at low exchange fractions is plausible, yet the plan underestimates practical linker-solubility/transport constraints and the possibility that even ‘non-coordinating’ solvents and mild heat can induce partial dissolution–recrystallization in Zn-carboxylate MOFs; the PDF/stoichiometry checks help, but the criteria may not fully distinguish subtle recrystallization from true SCSC. Finally, the pocket-density descriptor (ρpocket = xexchange × θC=N) is useful but incomplete: it ignores spatial correlations (clustering vs isolation) and local microenvironment distributions, which can dominate catalysis/ee in confined photoredox where exciton/radical migration lengths matter.

Hypothesis: A helically scrolled MOF nanotube derived from a pre-registered, carboxylate-latticed 2D coordination nanosheet can sustain morphology-retentive conversion into a porous Zr6-cluster–stitched framework if (and only if) the precursor nanosheet is reticularly matched to the Zr6O4(OH)4 connectivity and the conversion proceeds via kinetically controlled, surface-confined cluster nucleation rather than bulk single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SC–SC) exchange. In this architecture, directional ligand-to-metal/ligand-to-ligand charge-transfer (LMCT/LLCT) is not enforced by chirality alone but by a chemically encoded inner/outer surface redox asymmetry: asymmetric axial capping creates a permanent electrostatic potential gradient across the tube wall, while Zr6 stitching rigidifies registry and suppresses excimer-forming interlayer contacts. The result is (i) enhanced, tunable solid-state emission with reduced trap-mediated quenching and (ii) spatially vectorial charge separation that biases photogenerated electrons and holes toward chemically distinct inner versus outer surfaces, enabling measurable selectivity in CO2 photoreduction when catalytic sites are deliberately confined to one interface.
Plan:
Step 1 – Reticular precursor design with guaranteed Zr6 compatibility.
1.1 Ligand lattice pre-registration: Replace the generic salphen CP with a mixed-linker 2D coordination nanosheet built from (i) an atropisomeric, redox-active N2O2 chelating core (Ni(II) or Cu(II)) that defines in-plane conjugation and (ii) a co-planar, ditopic isophthalate-derived carboxylate linker whose O–O spacing (≈6.9–7.2 Å) and 120° geometry are matched to the equatorial edges of Zr6O4(OH)4 clusters. The carboxylates are positioned periodically (every ~1.5–2.0 nm) in the plane, forming a known (sql or kgm-type) 2D net that is crystallographically resolvable by GIWAXS/electron diffraction prior to scrolling.
1.2 Nanosheet formation: Grow 2–3 nm thick CP nanosheets by liquid–liquid interfacial coordination polymerization under modulator-free conditions to minimize defect density. Confirm in-plane order and lattice constants by GIWAXS and selected-area electron diffraction (SAED).

Step 2 – Deterministic helical scrolling with preserved lattice registry.
2.1 One-sided axial functionalization: Introduce 3–5% axial camphorsulfonate (or enantiopure menthoxyacetate) exclusively from the organic phase during interfacial growth to bind axial sites of Ni/Cu on only one face. This establishes a fixed dipolar and steric asymmetry without perturbing in-plane carboxylate registry.
2.2 Scrolling trigger: Apply a controlled solvent activity gradient (THF → MeCN/H2O, Δa_w quantified) to induce differential swelling. Helix pitch and diameter are tuned by sheet thickness and ionic strength, while in-plane diffraction is monitored to ensure lattice retention during scrolling.

Step 3 – Crystallographically defensible Zr6-cluster stitching (non-SC–SC).
3.1 Surface-confined Zr6 nucleation: Expose the helical CP scrolls to pre-formed Zr6O4(OH)4(modulator)x clusters (x = acetate/formate) in MeCN/H2O (≤10% H2O) at 50–70 °C. Use excess monocarboxylate modulator to slow ligand exchange, favoring stepwise substitution of modulators by pre-registered sheet carboxylates. This avoids uncontrolled Zr–O–Zr condensation.
3.2 Kinetic locking rather than bulk exchange: Zr6 clusters first bind within a single turn of the scroll, then progressively bridge adjacent turns only where lattice registry matches. Conversion is stopped at partial stitching densities (30–60%) to preserve porosity and avoid collapse.
3.3 Validation of registry: Compare in-plane GIWAXS/SAED before and after Zr6 incorporation; retention of peak positions (±2%) is required for pass. Loss of registry is a fail condition.

Step 4 – Proof of framework porosity vs. inter-scroll voids.
4.1 Gas sorption hierarchy: Measure N2 (77 K), Ar (87 K), CO2 (273/298 K), and Xe/Kr adsorption to extract pore-size distributions characteristic of Zr–carboxylate frameworks (≤2 nm). Contrast with collapsed-scroll controls.
4.2 Contrast-matched porosity tests: Perform positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS) or Xe NMR to distinguish intrinsic framework pores from mesoscopic voids between scroll turns.

Step 5 – Quantification of cross-wall redox asymmetry and CT directionality.
5.1 Surface potential mapping: Use Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) on sectioned nanotubes to map inner vs outer surface potentials; a ≥50–100 mV difference is targeted.
5.2 Depth-resolved composition: Apply angle-resolved XPS and ToF-SIMS to confirm asymmetric axial capping and Zr6 distribution across the wall.
5.3 Directional charge separation tests: Perform transient absorption spectroscopy with selective inner- or outer-surface quenchers (e.g., tethered viologen vs TEMPO). Faster quenching on one interface constitutes pass/fail evidence of vectorial CT.

Step 6 – CO2 photoreduction with enforced interface asymmetry.
6.1 Catalyst localization: Confine molecular Re(I) or Mn(I) bipyridine carbonyl catalysts to the inner surface only (1–2% sites) via pre-installed docking ligands. Outer surface remains catalyst-free.
6.2 Photocatalysis and causality: Measure CO/ HCOO− production under 13CO2. Correlate rates and selectivity with KPFM-measured potential gradients and CT lifetimes. Compare to symmetric (two-sided capped) and unscrolled controls to isolate the role of geometry-induced redox asymmetry.
Feasibility: This revision removes the chemically fragile SC–SC claim and replaces it with a kinetically and crystallographically defensible pathway rooted in reticular chemistry. By pre-designing a carboxylate lattice whose spacing and geometry are explicitly matched to Zr6 cluster connectivity, the proposal satisfies the reviewer’s demand for registry rather than assuming it. Surface-confined cluster nucleation using pre-formed Zr6 units and strong modulators is a known strategy in UiO-type post-synthetic modification and minimizes amorphization risks. Importantly, porosity is proven by multiple orthogonal techniques that discriminate framework pores from inter-scroll voids. The charge-transfer mechanism is no longer inferred from chirality alone: it is quantified via surface-potential mapping, depth-resolved spectroscopy, and directional quenching experiments that directly test inner/outer redox asymmetry. Finally, CO2 reduction selectivity is mechanistically tied to enforced interface chemistry (catalyst localization + potential gradient), not to helicity as an abstract concept. Together, these changes convert the highest-risk steps into testable, pass/fail milestones and tightly couple helical morphology, electronic structure, and catalytic outcome.
Critique: The proposal is unusually strong in experimental resolution: it defines lattice-matching targets, specifies nucleation control via pre-formed Zr6 clusters and modulators, and sets clear structural validation criteria (GIWAXS/SAED retention ±2%). The biggest scientific risk is mechanistic over-determination: (i) the assumption that partial Zr6 “stitching densities” of 30–60% will both preserve helical morphology and generate an internally connected, intrinsically microporous Zr–carboxylate framework is not yet chemically justified—partial crosslinking may yield a mechanically locked composite with inter-turn voids rather than a true Zr6-node framework; (ii) cross-wall electrostatic potential gradients measured by KPFM on sectioned nanotubes can be dominated by contact potential/work-function artifacts, charging, or thickness variations, so the claimed ≥50–100 mV may not uniquely report “inner vs outer redox asymmetry”; (iii) catalyst localization to the inner surface at 1–2% while keeping the outer surface catalyst-free is nontrivial in a porous, defect-bearing, partially stitched wall—diffusion/redistribution and unintended binding to Zr6 carboxylate sites could erase interface specificity; and (iv) the link from chirality/scrolling to suppression of excimer-forming contacts and improved emission is plausible but under-specified—no quantitative structural handle (interchromophore distance/orientation distribution) is proposed to connect stitching to excitonic coupling and trap suppression. Overall, the logic is coherent and testable, but several causal claims (true framework porosity; unambiguous vectorial CT; enforced interface-only catalysis) remain insufficiently de-risked by controls that distinguish alternative explanations.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a permanently porous, pressure- and analyte-responsive carboxylate MOF can be rationally programmed to exhibit cooperative gate-opening via a crystallographically enforced alternation of carboxylate binding modes that is symmetry-required rather than kinetically imposed during growth. Specifically, we propose a hexacarboxylate linker and single-metal, high-connectivity Zr6-based secondary building unit (SBU) that crystallizes in a low-symmetry (orthorhombic or monoclinic) space group containing two inequivalent carboxylate coordination environments per linker: (i) rigid, coplanar μ2-η1:η1 Zr–carboxylates that define the load-bearing backbone and enforce permanent porosity, and (ii) symmetry-distinct μ2-η2:η1 carboxylates associated with sterically frustrated binding pockets that permit pressure-induced torsional reorientation. This alternation is encoded by linker topology and space-group constraints (not by growth-layer modulation), yielding a predictable superstructure with crystallographically resolvable order parameters (carboxylate tilt angle, aperture width). Upon hydrostatic gas loading (N2, H2), collective elastic coupling between these inequivalent sites produces a bistable free-energy landscape with a quantifiable gate-opening pressure and hysteresis. Polar analytes (amines, carbonyl VOCs) selectively stabilize the open state via directional host–guest interactions, thereby amplifying the structural transition and enabling quantitative chemical sensing intrinsically linked to hydrogen sorption.
Plan:
1. Crystallographic and chemical design (enforceable structural program):
1.1 Linker design: Synthesize a rigid acetylene-centered hexacarboxylate ligand (LH6) in which three carboxylates are directly conjugated to the C≡C core (planar, high torsional penalty) and three are appended via short –CH2– spacers (rotationally compliant). The linker geometry is chosen to be incompatible with high-symmetry cubic nets, forcing crystallization in an orthorhombic/monoclinic lattice with two symmetry-inequivalent carboxylate sites.
1.2 Node selection (de-risked SBU): Employ a single-metal Zr6O4(OH)4 carboxylate cluster (UiO-type family) with full 12-connectivity to avoid metal scrambling. Directional compliance is introduced by linker asymmetry rather than heterometallicity. Defect concentration is minimized via excess monotopic acid modulation and verified quantitatively.
1.3 Target topology and symmetry: Reticular analysis will target a non-cubic (e.g., shp- or csq-derived) topology in space groups such as C2/c or Pnma, where two crystallographically distinct carboxylate coordination modes are symmetry-mandated. Expected superstructure reflections and inequivalent C=O environments are predicted a priori.

2. Verification of structural alternation:
2.1 SCXRD: Solve and refine single-crystal structures to explicitly resolve inequivalent carboxylate binding modes, linker torsion angles, and aperture dimensions. Collect high-redundancy data to detect weak superstructure reflections; analyze anisotropic displacement parameters and residual density for incipient disorder.
2.2 Complementary spectroscopy: Use solid-state 13C CP-MAS NMR to distinguish inequivalent carboxylate carbon environments; IR spectroscopy to resolve split νas(COO−)/νs(COO−) bands corresponding to different binding modes.
2.3 Defect quantification: Employ 1H NMR of digested samples and TGA to quantify missing-linker defects; target <5% defect density.

3. Quantitative mechanics and thermodynamics:
3.1 Elastic modeling: Calculate elastic constants from DFT (periodic) and validate via nanoindentation on single crystals. Identify soft modes associated with compliant carboxylates.
3.2 Free-energy landscapes: Perform DFT-based static calculations and classical MD with enhanced sampling to map free-energy profiles as a function of aperture angle under hydrostatic pressure and guest loading (N2, H2, NH3). Predict gate-opening pressures and hysteresis widths.
3.3 Symmetry change prediction: Identify expected symmetry lowering or lattice strain signatures accompanying the closed→open transition to guide operando diffraction.

4. Operando adsorption and SC–SC transformation studies:
4.1 Gas adsorption: Measure N2 isotherms at 77 K and H2 isotherms up to 120 bar at 77 K and 87 K. Identify stepped isotherms and hysteresis corresponding to cooperative opening.
4.2 In situ SCXRD: Conduct high-pressure SCXRD under N2 and H2 to directly correlate adsorption inflection points with changes in unit-cell parameters, carboxylate tilt angles, and guest locations.

5. Chemical sensing as a flow-through, quantitative experiment:
5.1 Device architecture: Fabricate oriented polycrystalline films on interdigitated electrodes via solvothermal epitaxial growth from the same phase.
5.2 Operando sensing: Perform flow-through sensing experiments with controlled analyte concentrations (amines, acetone) under dry and humid conditions (0–80% RH). Metrics: limit of detection (ppb), response/recovery times, selectivity factors over H2/N2, and cycling stability.
5.3 Structure–signal correlation: Correlate impedance/optical responses with the SCXRD-defined structural order parameter (aperture angle or unit-cell strain) to establish causality.
Feasibility: This revised strategy directly addresses reviewer concerns by replacing speculative growth-layer alternation with a symmetry-enforced, crystallographically verifiable alternation of carboxylate binding modes that is well precedented in low-symmetry Zr-carboxylate MOFs. By eliminating heterometallic SBUs, the proposal avoids metal scrambling while retaining permanent porosity and SC–SC robustness characteristic of UiO-type frameworks (Asset 3). The use of rigid acetylene-linked carboxylates draws on established high-surface-area, high-pressure hydrogen storage principles (Asset 4), while introducing controlled mechanical compliance analogous to linker-rotation-driven breathing phenomena (Asset 1). Quantitative elastic and free-energy modeling provides predicted transition pressures and hysteresis, strengthening mechanistic sufficiency. Finally, defining sensing as an operando, flow-through measurement with explicit performance metrics and direct correlation to SCXRD-resolved structural parameters aligns the proposal with best practices in MOF-based chemical sensing and thin-film integration (Asset 2), ensuring both conceptual rigor and experimental realism.
Critique: The proposal is technically ambitious and largely well-instrumented (SCXRD/operando SCXRD, adsorption, defect quantification, DFT/MD, nanoindentation, device metrics). The main weaknesses are (i) an overconfident claim that the linker will “force” orthorhombic/monoclinic symmetry and “symmetry-mandate” two carboxylate binding modes—this is plausible but not demonstrated as inevitable versus disorder, partial occupancy, or alternative nets; (ii) insufficient de-risking of single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SC–SC) transformations under 77 K cryogenic adsorption and up to 120 bar H2, where crystal integrity and equilibration can fail; (iii) a gap between the hypothesized cooperative elastic coupling and the experimental observables—stepped isotherms/hysteresis can arise from defects, domain formation, or crystal-size effects, so more discriminating validation is needed (e.g., variable-temperature isotherms for thermodynamic parameters; calorimetry; diffraction-based phase-fraction tracking); and (iv) the required concept “layer-by-layer growth” is not actually implemented—epitaxial solvothermal film growth is different from LbL methods and has different controllability over orientation/defects, which matters for sensing reproducibility. Overall, the mechanistic direction is strong, but the symmetry/topology determinism and the operando structure–property causality require tighter proof and controls.

Hypothesis: A Y-shaped catalytic hairpin assembly (Y-CHA) circuit nucleated from a Co-MOF-on-COF ultrathin heterointerface will produce a superlinear EIS response because the Y-CHA product is engineered to (i) physically and coordinatively crosslink adjacent Co open-metal-sites (OMS) and (ii) gate ionic/mediator access through the MOF meso/microporous shell, creating a connectivity transition (“percolation threshold”) in transport pathways. Mechanistically, the proposal explicitly separates three coupled but distinguishable contributors to the impedance signal: (A) electron-transfer physics (film/charge-transport + interfacial k0), (B) ionic/pore-access (diffusion/migration through a porous shell, pore constriction), and (C) electrostatic repulsion (Donnan exclusion of charged mediators by the increasingly polyanionic DNA layer). The revised design resolves reviewer concerns by: (1) providing an explicit electron-transport pathway through a redox-hopping Co(II)/Co(III) network and/or embedded redox mediators (catechol/ferrocene) within a ≤20 nm Co-MOF shell so film resistance does not dominate Rct; (2) operationally defining and measuring the percolation threshold using orthogonal observables (QCM-D/SPR mass uptake, AFM thickness/roughness, and XPS P/S elemental quantitation for crosslink density), then correlating these to nonlinear Rct; (3) deconvoluting pore-gating from electrostatics by performing EIS in oppositely charged mediators ([Fe(CN)6]3−/4− vs [Ru(NH3)6]3+/2+) plus a mediator-free surface-tethered ferrocene readout; and (4) making LC–MS/MS stoichiometric to target binding by placing a single cleavable isotopic reporter on the surface initiator (one initiator released/cleaved per captured target event) rather than on amplified Y-CHA products, thereby enabling absolute ‘captured miR-133a equivalents’ calibration or, alternatively, clearly framing MS as qualitative verification if stoichiometry controls fail.
Plan:
Step 1 — Materials architecture with defined transport pathway (addresses Critique #1).
1.1 COF underlayer (chemically addressable, thin, continuous):
- Electrode: Au (for SPR/QCM-D compatibility) and glassy carbon (for robustness). Use identical geometric area and include Au/Ti for adhesion if needed.
- COF: nitrogen-rich, π-conjugated TPN-like COF grown as a thin film (target thickness 10–30 nm; rms roughness <3 nm) via interfacial or surface-confined polymerization to minimize insulating thickness.
- Functional handles: incorporate a controlled fraction (1–5%) of aldehyde- or carboxyl-terminated monomers (or post-synthetic modification) to tune wettability and reduce nonspecific serum adsorption.
1.2 Co-MOF-on-COF ultrathin shell with redox-hopping support:
- Grow Co-MOF shell by layer-by-layer (LBL) room-temperature growth to control thickness precisely: target 5, 10, 20 nm shells (not 50 nm by default). Stop when continuous coverage is achieved (AFM step height + SEM continuity).
- MOF chemistry: Co(II) nodes + rigid aromatic dicarboxylate ligand (e.g., 2,6-naphthalenedicarboxylate) to promote π-stacking/packing and improve electronic coupling; activate to expose Co OMS (solvent exchange + mild thermal/vacuum activation compatible with film).
- Built-in redox mediator option (explicit): co-introduce a small fraction (0.5–2 mol%) of redox-active linker (catechol/quinone-like or ferrocene-dicarboxylate analogue) during LBL cycles to enable defined redox-hopping across the ultrathin MOF shell; verify incorporation by XPS/ToF-SIMS.
1.3 Mixed-valence tuning with an explicit electrochemical model:
- Create controlled Co(II)/Co(III) ratio via potentiostatic conditioning in benign electrolyte (e.g., phosphate-buffered saline without halides that strongly complex Co) using fixed potentials and times; quantify Co valence by XPS/XANES.
- Replace the single Randles assumption with a porous-electrode / transmission line model (TLM) fit: extract film resistance (Rf), distributed charge-transfer (Rct,dist), and CPE dispersion (α) to explicitly test whether the observed ‘steepness’ arises from transport limitations vs interfacial blocking.
- Thickness dependence: measure EIS vs shell thickness (5/10/20 nm) to confirm that Rf scales with thickness while the nonlinear Rct jump correlates with crosslinking metrics (Step 3), not merely with thickness.

Step 2 — DNA anchoring redesigned to preserve accessibility and reduce fouling (addresses Critique #3).
2.1 Anti-fouling and controlled probe spacing:
- Introduce a short mixed monolayer strategy at the Co-MOF surface: co-immobilize initiator strands with a diluent (PEGylated or zwitterionic short oligo/thiol surrogate) to control probe density and reduce serum adsorption.
- Use a single primary anchoring mode to avoid overconstraint: prefer Co–imidazole coordination at OMS with a spacer (e.g., hexaethylene glycol or polyT) to lift the initiator away from the surface; keep π–π/COF interactions secondary (non-covalent) rather than a required attachment.
- Quantify surface density and accessibility by: (i) fluorescently labeled initiator calibration; (ii) SPR association kinetics; (iii) nuclease/strand-displacement accessibility assay.
2.2 Competitive coordination/fouling stress tests (built-in controls):
- Challenge with histidine/imidazole (1–10 mM) and EDTA (0.1–1 mM) under controlled conditions to determine how much of the signal depends on Co–DNA coordination vs mere adsorption.
- Serum fouling panel: 10% and 50% serum exposure, with and without BSA/casein blocking; track baseline drift in Rf and CPE to separate fouling capacitance effects from true Rct changes.

Step 3 — Y-CHA circuit engineered for coordination crosslinking and independently quantifiable threshold (addresses Critique #2).
3.1 Y-CHA design with crosslinkable arms (chemically explicit):
- H1/H2 sequences selected for miR-133a triggering with target recycling; design for minimal off-target to close miRNA family members using mismatch discrimination in toehold region.
- Y-product arms:
  (A) Imidazole-bearing domain: multiple imidazole-modified nucleotides (e.g., imidazole-dU) spaced to enable multidentate binding to Co OMS.
  (B) Phosphorothioate (PS) tract: 6–10 consecutive PS linkages positioned to chelate Co and bridge nearby nodes; use a defined PS count to enable XPS quantification of S.
  (C) Optional inert arm for sterics: polyT/PEG segment to increase excluded volume and enhance pore constriction without adding charge-binding ambiguity.
- Negative controls: identical Y-CHA lacking imidazole/PS features (no crosslinking), and a linear hybridization probe with equivalent net charge.
3.2 Operational definition of percolation threshold (quantitative criterion):
- Define the threshold as the surface state where the second derivative of log(Rct) vs X becomes positive and maximal (inflection to superlinear regime), where X is an independent coverage/crosslink metric (mass uptake or elemental ratio), not miRNA concentration.
- Independent observables for X:
  (i) QCM-D on Au: Δf/ΔD to obtain areal mass uptake and viscoelasticity during Y-CHA growth.
  (ii) SPR on Au: resonance shift to confirm binding kinetics and surface coverage trends.
  (iii) AFM: thickness increase (Δh) and roughness changes mapping the emergence of a connected layer.
  (iv) XPS elemental quantitation: P (DNA backbone) and S (PS tracts) normalized to Co to estimate crosslink density per area; track S/P ratio to verify PS incorporation independent of total DNA.
- Correlate the onset of nonlinearity in EIS with the above metrics to claim a true ‘connectivity transition’ rather than a smooth surface-coverage increase.

Step 4 — Mechanistic deconvolution package mandated by reviewers (explicit separation A/B/C).
4.1 Multi-mediator EIS to separate electrostatics from pore-gating:
- Perform EIS in:
  (i) Anionic outer-sphere: [Fe(CN)6]3−/4− (electrostatic repulsion expected to be strong).
  (ii) Cationic outer-sphere: [Ru(NH3)6]3+/2+ (electrostatic attraction expected).
- Compare ΔRct signatures: pore-gating should increase Rct in both mediators (direction-independent), while pure electrostatics should show opposite or strongly asymmetric behavior.
4.2 Mediator-free interfacial redox to isolate electron-transfer physics:
- Introduce a surface-tethered ferrocene (Fc) reporter (either Fc-initiator strand or Fc-diluent strand) such that the Fc is proximal to the electrode and reports local electron transfer independent of diffusion through pores.
- Measure Fc EIS/voltammetry before/after Y-CHA: if Fc kinetics remain stable while solution-mediator Rct jumps, the dominant mechanism is pore-access gating rather than a global loss of electronic conductivity.
4.3 Film resistance and distributed kinetics (avoid overfitting Randles):
- Use TLM/porous electrode model fits to extract Rf and distributed Rct; validate Rf independently via conductive AFM (nanoscale) and/or four-point probe on larger-area films where feasible.
- Thickness series (5/10/20 nm) under identical Y-CHA conditions to confirm that superlinearity appears at a similar coverage metric X, not simply at a particular thickness.

Step 5 — EIS readout protocol and analytical claims.
5.1 EIS acquisition and fitting:
- Frequency range and perturbation amplitude fixed; report fit quality metrics and parameter confidence intervals.
- Primary outputs: distributed Rct (or pore-associated charge-transfer resistance), Rf, and low-frequency phase angle; treat changes in CPE (α) as diagnostics for fouling/heterogeneity.
5.2 Performance evaluation:
- Determine LOD/LOQ in buffer and serum; dynamic range; mismatch selectivity against miR-21/miR-499 and single-base mismatches; regeneration using mild strand displacement and re-activation of Co OMS (validated by XPS).

Step 6 — LC–MS/MS orthogonal verification with explicit stoichiometry (addresses Critique #4).
6.1 Stoichiometric MS design (preferred):
- Place a single cleavable isotopic reporter on the surface initiator strand (not on Y-CHA products). Design the sensing so that target binding triggers one-time initiator processing (e.g., target-assisted cleavage/strand displacement releasing exactly one reporter per captured target) while Y-CHA amplification proceeds without generating additional reporters.
- After EIS, cleave/release the reporter quantitatively (photocleavage or chemical cleavage) and quantify by LC–MS/MS with an isotopically labeled internal standard.
- Validate stoichiometry in a calibration series by comparing MS reporter counts to independently quantified target inputs under conditions where amplification is active vs suppressed.
6.2 If stoichiometry cannot be guaranteed (fallback):
- Reframe LC–MS/MS as qualitative/confirmatory (presence/identity) and semi-quantitative (trend) rather than absolute ‘captured equivalents’; explicitly report amplification factor uncertainty.

Step 7 — Decision gates and risk mitigation.
7.1 If Rf dominates (high film resistance):
- Reduce MOF thickness, increase redox-linker fraction, or switch to a more conductive MOF chemistry while retaining Co OMS at the outer surface (core-shell concept preserved).
7.2 If electrostatics dominate (anionic vs cationic mediator diverge strongly):
- Increase ionic strength, introduce charge-neutral spacers, and rely on mediator-free Fc reporting plus pore-access metrics.
7.3 If serum fouling overwhelms signals:
- Add zwitterionic/PEG passivation, optimize probe spacing, and include pre-filtration or microfluidic washing; verify with QCM-D dissipation and XPS N/C ratios.

Deliverables (explicit evidence chain):
- Proof of transport pathway: Rf vs thickness (TLM + c-AFM/four-point) and stable Fc kinetics.
- Proof of pore-gating vs electrostatics: consistent Rct increase in both anionic and cationic mediators + Fc control.
- Proof of percolation-like transition: correlated nonlinear Rct onset with QCM-D/SPR/AFM/XPS-derived coverage/crosslink density threshold.
- Proof of MS linkage: validated reporter stoichiometry or explicit qualitative framing.
Feasibility:
1) Electron-transport feasibility (resolves ‘insulating COF + MOF shell’ concern): The revised architecture constrains the Co-MOF shell to ≤20 nm and optionally embeds a small fraction of redox-active linkers to support redox-hopping transport. Mixed-valence Co(II)/Co(III) is no longer asserted as a vague ‘steepness’ enhancer; it is quantified (XPS/XANES) and modeled with a porous-electrode/TLM framework that separates film resistance from interfacial charge transfer. This directly addresses mediator choice and CPE dispersion confounders.

2) Mechanistic proof of superlinearity (resolves percolation ambiguity): The percolation threshold is operationally defined using independent coverage/crosslink metrics (QCM-D/SPR mass uptake, AFM morphology, and XPS P/S-to-Co ratios). Nonlinearity is claimed only when the Rct inflection coincides with a threshold in these independent observables and persists across mediator charge sign.
