Hypothesis: A solvent-filled, heterometallic Fe/Co rod-SBU “chain–pillar” MOF can be made intrinsically collapse-resistant if (i) topochemical constraints (pendant-group proximity and orientation) are verified crystallographically in the solvated state, (ii) open metal sites are deliberately capped to prevent catalyst poisoning and uncontrolled coordination chemistry, and (iii) an intrapore covalent crosslinking reaction is selected that is (a) Cu-free / metathesis-free or uses a protected catalyst and (b) sufficiently strain-tolerant to proceed via a programmed single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SCSC) transformation. Mechanistically, solvent-exchange collapse in rod-MOFs is initiated by capillary-pressure-driven linker hinging and node shear; adding a sparse, percolating covalent ‘brace network’ converts the lattice from purely coordinative connectivity to a coordinative–covalent hybrid, raising the shear modulus (G) and increasing the collapse pressure threshold. The Fe/Co ratio is not assumed to monotonically control stiffness; rather, it is treated as a coupled control variable that modulates (1) node Lewis acidity and ligand-exchange kinetics (thereby controlling how strongly temporary capping ligands protect the node and how readily the node tolerates crosslinking reagents), (2) defect chemistry (missing-linker/terminal ligand populations that soften the lattice), and (3) breathing amplitude that perturbs pendant-group distances. By staging (a) structure-guided crosslinker selection/redesign, (b) a minimal chemistry screen in homometal parents under capped-node conditions, and (c) direct mechanical readouts (nanoindentation/Brillouin) before expanding the full Fe/Co matrix, we de-risk the two highest-failure modes identified by reviewers: (i) catalyst deactivation/poisoning or framework damage, and (ii) insufficient topochemical alignment for high-yield inter-linker coupling. After ‘locking’, CH4 pressure-swing cycling will be performed under explicitly controlled dry vs humid conditions, enabling separation of adsorption-strain-driven damage from hydrolysis/impurity-driven decomposition; the resulting composition–structure–mechanics–stability map will identify the Fe/Co window that maximizes (crosslink density × modulus gain × surface-area retention) while preserving crystallinity and CH4 working capacity.
Plan:
Stage 0 (Go/No-Go gate design; weeks 1–10): determine whether topochemistry + benign intrapore coupling + SCSC retention is achievable in at least one parent composition before any full Fe/Co matrix.

0.1 Select an implementable rod-MOF family and define node-capping strategy up front.
- Target topology: MIL-53/MIL-68-like 1D channels built from infinite M–O–C rods (carboxylate chains) + pillar/linker.
- Metals: Fe(III) and Co(II/III) in mixed-metal rods; initial de-risking uses homometal Fe-only and Co-only analogues.
- Node-site protection (mandatory): install labile, monodentate capping ligands to occupy open metal sites during crosslinking to prevent catalyst sequestration and uncontrolled coordination. Two orthogonal caps will be screened:
  (A) pyridine-N-oxide (PNO, weakly coordinating, displaceable) or DMF retained at nodes (baseline), and
  (B) acetate/benzoate terminal ligands introduced via modulated synthesis to pre-saturate labile sites.
- Verification of capping: quantify terminal ligands/defects by quantitative digest NMR (linker:cap ratio) and thermogravimetric titration (mass loss assignment to caps/solvent), supported by XPS (N 1s for PNO) and EXAFS for coordination-number changes.
- Go/No-Go criterion G0: capped-node samples must show no significant loss of crystallinity after 72 h soak in the intended reaction solvent at reaction temperature (≤60 °C), judged by PXRD peak integrity (≥90% relative intensity retained) and unchanged unit cell within ±0.5%.

Stage 1 (Topochemical feasibility; weeks 4–14): crystallographically prove pendant-group geometry in the solvent-filled state and under solvent swaps.

1.1 Solve at least one solvent-filled crystal structure (as-synthesized) for one composition.
- Choose the composition that yields the largest, highest-quality crystals first (anticipated: homometal Co-MOF often crystallizes better; if not, use Fe-MOF).
- Crystal size/quality window for SCXRD: target 50–150 µm single crystals, low mosaicity (<0.5° preferred). Establish growth conditions by modulated solvothermal synthesis (acid modulator equivalents varied 5–50 eq) to tune size.
- Data: SCXRD structure with resolved pendant groups (or partially occupied disorder model) and channel solvent.

1.2 Quantify the ‘reactive distance distribution’ and breathing sensitivity.
- Extract across-channel pendant–pendant distances (d) and relative approach angles (θ) for the intended coupling reaction (e.g., S···C for thiol–ene preorganization, azide–alkyne proximity for click-like, alkene–alkene proximity for [2+2]/metathesis).
- Perform solvent-dependent unit-cell + geometry mapping by sequential, gentle solvent replacement while keeping crystals solvated (e.g., mother liquor → DMF → MeCN → acetone), collecting SCXRD where possible or high-resolution PXRD + Pawley/Rietveld to track cell changes.
- Go/No-Go criterion G1: identify at least one solvent condition in which a majority population of pendant pairs satisfy d ≤ 6.5 Å (for flexible bis-thiol bridging/thiol–ene proximity) or d ≤ 7–10 Å (for a designed bifunctional crosslinker length), and where breathing does not broaden d beyond a bimodal distribution that would preclude percolation (operationally: standard deviation of d across symmetry-unique pairs ≤ 1.5 Å).

1.3 Crosslinker-length selection/redesign based on measured geometry.
- If pendant pairs are too far: redesign linker to enforce proximity (e.g., move pendant group from meta to ortho relative to carboxylate to bias inward projection; incorporate a rigid spacer to reduce conformational freedom).
- If pendant pairs are too close and risk pore blocking: select a shorter, more flexible crosslinker to avoid dense network formation.

Stage 2 (Minimal chemistry screen in homometal parents; weeks 10–26): demonstrate intrapore coupling under capped-node conditions with SCSC/PXRD retention before expanding to Fe/Co series.

2.1 Replace high-risk CuAAC and Grubbs metathesis with a staged reaction screen that prioritizes catalyst-tolerant, strain-tolerant, Cu-free pathways.
- Primary route (Cu-free, node-benign): photoinitiated thiol–ene coupling.
  • Linker pendant group: terminal alkene preferred for thiol–ene.
  • Diffuse a dithiol crosslinker (HS–(CH2)n–SH; n chosen from Stage 1 geometry; start n=2,4,6) into solvent-filled crystals.
  • Initiation: 365–405 nm LED irradiation with a pore-diffusible photoinitiator (e.g., DMPA at low mM) in MeCN or acetone; temperature 25–35 °C.
  • Rationale: radical thiol–ene is tolerant of carboxylates and avoids strong metal-binding catalysts; often proceeds with low strain penalty and high functional-group tolerance.
- Secondary route (latent crosslinker, thermal trigger): incorporate pendant groups that undergo thermally activated cycloaddition without metal catalysts.
  • Example: furan–maleimide Diels–Alder (DA) pair split across linkers (requires dual-linker strategy) or a masked nitrile imine precursor for photoinduced 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition.
  • Trigger at 40–80 °C (DA) or UV (photo-click), all under capped-node conditions.
- Tertiary route (only if needed, and only after soak-stability is proven): Cu-free strain-promoted azide–alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC).
  • Use cyclooctyne-bearing pendant groups (linker redesign) + difunctional azide crosslinker; eliminates Cu entirely.
  • This is retained as a contingency due to synthetic overhead.

2.2 Diffusion timescale and reaction uniformity control.
- Measure reagent uptake kinetics using gravimetry or UV–vis depletion (for initiator) and/or confocal Raman mapping (alkene band intensity vs position) across a single crystal.
- Establish diffusion time t90 (time to reach 90% uptake) for each crystal size; restrict SCSC experiments to crystals where t90 ≤ 12 h to avoid gradients.
- Go/No-Go criterion G2: post-reaction crystals must retain sharp PXRD peaks (FWHM increase ≤ 20%), maintain unit cell within ±1%, and show ≥30% conversion of pendant groups (digest NMR) without evidence of linker cleavage (LC-MS of digests: no new low-mass fragments above 5% relative abundance).

2.3 SCSC monitoring strategy that does not rely solely on in situ SCXRD.
- In situ: high-resolution PXRD during reaction (capillary setup, solvent-saturated) to monitor phase purity/unit-cell drift.
- Ex situ: SCXRD on a subset of crystals that survive (not mandatory for every condition).
- Spectroscopy: Raman/IR (loss of C=C or appearance of thioether C–S band); solid-state 13C NMR confirming new bond formation.

Stage 3 (Mechanical hardening validation; weeks 18–36): directly measure modulus gain and tie it to stitch density and collapse threshold.

3.1 Mechanical proxies.
- Nanoindentation on oriented single crystals (if size permits): measure reduced modulus (Er) pre/post crosslinking; target ≥25% increase as meaningful hardening.
- If crystals are too small: Brillouin light scattering on crystal aggregates to extract longitudinal/transverse sound velocities and estimate elastic constants; complement with AFM modulus mapping on microcrystals embedded in epoxy.

3.2 Collapse threshold mapping.
- Variable-pressure in situ PXRD during controlled drying (stepwise reduction of solvent vapor pressure) to detect gate-closure/collapse onset.
- Surface area retention: N2 (77 K) and Ar (87 K) BET; compare to non-stitched controls.
- Go/No-Go criterion G3: crosslinked sample must retain ≥80% of the parent’s solvated-porosity-derived accessible volume (operationally: ≥80% of BET area of the best-activated control using the same drying protocol) and shift collapse onset to lower vapor pressure (or higher applied capillary stress) by ≥30% relative to non-stitched analog.

Stage 4 (Only after passing G1–G3): expand to Fe/Co composition matrix with defect and node-chemistry covariates explicitly measured (weeks 28–60).

4.1 Composition set and synthesis.
- Ratios: Fe/Co = 0/1, 1/9, 1/4, 1/2, 1/1, 2/1, 1/0 (as originally proposed), but synthesized in two waves:
  • Wave A (3 compositions): Co-only, Fe/Co=1/4, Fe-only.
  • Wave B (remaining): fill in after identifying the ‘safe’ crosslinking window.
- Control defect density via modulator equivalents; track missing-linker populations via quantitative digest NMR and TGA-based cap quantification.
- Metal distribution/speciation: ICP-OES for bulk; STEM-EDS for homogeneity; 57Fe Mössbauer + Co K-edge XANES/EXAFS to assign oxidation/spin states and coordination.

4.2 Crosslinking under the validated chemistry and capped-node condition.
- Apply the best-performing route from Stage 2; keep reaction conditions fixed to isolate composition effects.
- Quantify stitch density (digest NMR, solid-state NMR, XPS) and correlate with mechanical and sorption outcomes.

Stage 5 (CH4 adsorption/cycling with dry vs humid separation; weeks 40–72): isolate strain-driven effects from hydrolysis/impurities.

5.1 Gas quality and water control.
- Dry CH4 spec: use 6.0-grade CH4; pass through additional purifier; continuously monitor H2O with an online hygrometer at the instrument inlet/outlet.
- Define conditions:
  • “Dry”: H2O ≤ 1 ppm.
  • “Humid”: controlled 200–500 ppm H2O (and a higher-stress condition at ~1000 ppm) using a calibrated humidification loop.
- Analyze impurities (O2/CO2) by inline GC if possible; otherwise batch certificate + purifier performance logs.

5.2 Cycling protocol.
- CH4 isotherms at 273 and 298 K up to 65 bar.
- Pressure-swing cycling: 65→5 bar, ≥50 cycles dry and ≥50 cycles humid, identical ramp rates and dwell times.
- In situ PXRD under CH4 pressure for representative samples to monitor reversible breathing vs irreversible collapse.

5.3 Decomposition/defect propagation diagnostics.
- Post-cycling: BET area, pore-size distribution, PXRD.
- Chemical stability: TGA-DSC (inert/air), TGA-MS for fragments, LC-MS of digested linkers, EXAFS for node rearrangement, ICP of leached metals after humid exposure.
- Model includes defect density and capping-ligand population as covariates to avoid attributing all effects to Fe/Co ratio.

Deliverable: a composition–structure–stitch density–elastic modulus–collapse threshold–CH4 working capacity map identifying an Fe/Co window where (i) stitch conversion is high without SCSC loss, (ii) modulus gain is measurable, (iii) activation without supercritical CO2 yields high retained surface area, and (iv) CH4 cycling stability is limited by strain rather than hydrolysis (quantified by dry vs humid divergence).
Feasibility:
This revision explicitly addresses the review board’s feasibility gaps by adding staged de-risking gates, chemistry alternatives, node-protection, quantitative mechanics, and humidity-controlled CH4 testing.

(1) Topochemical constraints are no longer assumed: Stage 1 requires solving a solvent-filled crystal structure and quantifying pendant-pair distances/angles under multiple solvent states. Crosslinker length (or linker redesign) is chosen from measured geometry, directly satisfying the directive to prove inter-linker proximity in breathing rod-MOFs before committing to a composition matrix.

(2) Stitching chemistry is de-risked away from the two highest-risk catalytic assumptions (in-node CuAAC and ppm Grubbs metathesis). The primary screen uses photoinitiated thiol–ene (Cu-free, tolerant of carboxylates), while latent thermally/photochemically triggered options and SPAAC remain as contingencies. This directly mitigates risks of Cu sequestration/poisoning, uncontrolled metal-mediated nucleation, and metathesis catalyst deactivation by Fe/Co carboxylate environments.

(3) Open-metal-site poisoning and framework damage are proactively controlled via deliberate, quantified node capping (PNO or carboxylate terminals) plus mandatory soak-stability tests with PXRD/XANES/EXAFS validation, aligning with the directive to demonstrate catalyst/structure compatibility rather than assuming it.

(4) Mechanical hardening is made quantitative: modulus gain is measured (nanoindentation or Brillouin) and explicitly correlated with stitch density and collapse threshold (variable-pressure in situ PXRD during drying). This supplies the missing mechanical proxy for the shear-modulus premise and ties it to the functional outcome (surface-area retention) rather than relying on qualitative arguments.

(5) CH4-induced effects are separated from hydrolysis/impurity-driven degradation by explicit gas specs, online water-ppm monitoring, and parallel dry vs humid cycling under identical pressure swings, with defect density and terminal-ligand populations treated as covariates. This directly addresses the reviewer’s concern that “CH4-induced decomposition” can be confounded by moisture.

Integration with provided literature assets: Asset 2 motivates that activation protocol improvements alone cannot reliably prevent collapse; therefore, the proposal shifts the locus of control to pre-activation internal mechanical reinforcement. Asset 3 supports the premise that solvent-handling and post-synthetic transformations can preserve porosity and stability when designed to avoid decomposition pathways; here, SCSC-compatible intrapore locking is explicitly engineered with strain-tolerant chemistry and capped nodes. Asset 4 underscores that oxidative/hydrolytic environment changes can catastrophically reduce surface area and adsorption; accordingly, we incorporate humidity-controlled cycling and chemical-state diagnostics. Asset 1 establishes that Fe/Co ratio can strongly modulate morphology/porosity; in this proposal, Fe/Co is treated mechanistically and quantitatively through its effects on node chemistry, defect populations, breathing, and ultimately stitch yield and modulus gain—validated experimentally rather than assumed.

Overall, the concept chain remains identical (Fe/Co rod-MOF → solvent-filled intrapore covalent ‘locking’ → activation without collapse → CH4 cycling stability), but the highest-risk elements are now front-loaded into minimal go/no-go experiments with explicit quantitative criteria before expanding scope.
Critique: Methodologically, the staged de-risking with quantitative gates is strong and addresses the two dominant failure modes (misalignment and node/catalyst incompatibility). However, several key chemical/structural uncertainties remain under-specified for a rod-SBU Fe/Co system: (i) the actual identity/stoichiometry/charge balance of the heterometallic rod node and where “open metal sites” exist in the solvated structure is not pinned down, yet capping strategy, defect accounting, and crosslinking compatibility all depend on it; (ii) the primary thiol–ene route introduces plausible side reactions in redox-active Fe/Co carboxylate environments (thiyl radical quenching at metals, thiol coordination/displacement of caps, oxidative disulfide formation, radical damage to linkers), but the plan lacks explicit control experiments/analytics to distinguish true inter-linker stitching from thiol adsorption, chain transfer, or pore-filling; (iii) the percolation/‘sparse brace network’ premise is asserted but not quantitatively connected to a required conversion threshold, crosslink topology, and expected modulus gain—without a minimal mechanical model, the ≥25% modulus target and ≥30% conversion gate risk being arbitrary; (iv) SCSC is treated as a major objective, but rod-MOF breathing/disorder may preclude reliable pendant-pair statistics from SCXRD in many realistic cases (partial occupancy, dynamic disorder), so the proposal should define what “success” looks like if only high-resolution PXRD + spectroscopic constraints are achievable. Overall the concept chain is preserved and the engineering plan is credible, but the mechanistic link from chemistry → verified covalent network architecture → quantified modulus/collapse improvement needs tighter, falsifiable structure–property predictions.

Hypothesis: Chloroform (CHCl3) can be detected with a higher and more reproducible turn-on fluorescence quantum yield in NUS-1a by converting its AIE-active tetraphenylethene (TPE/DPEB) environment into a geometry-programmed host via **intrapore covalent phenyl-ring bracing** that (a) raises the torsional barriers of phenyl rotors (reducing non-radiative decay, knr) and (b) narrows/homogenizes the **pore aperture distribution** toward the kinetic-diameter regime relevant to CHCl3, thereby increasing CHCl3 residence time and occupancy at emissive sites. This proposal explicitly separates three contributing effects—(1) intrinsic rigidification by bracing, (2) pore-aperture redistribution/size-sieving, and (3) guest-assisted rigidification—by using a geometry-constrained crosslink design with a pre-registered conversion window that preserves accessible porosity, definitive chemical proof of covalent bracing (digest-and-analyze + isotopic mapping), and orthogonal controls that decouple crosslinking from catalyst exposure, thermal/solvent history, or external pore fouling. Mechanistically, the refined approach overcomes reviewer-identified feasibility risks by (i) precomputing feasible intrapore coupling pairs and selecting crosslinkers with a narrow length tolerance matched to those distances, (ii) enforcing intrapore selectivity through external-surface passivation + diffusion-bounded kinetics + low-conversion targets, and (iii) using a MOF-compatible click-chemistry contingency (thiol–ene or CuAAC) that avoids strongly basic/wet conditions that can destabilize Zn4O-carboxylate nodes.
Plan:
Step 0 — Pre-registered geometry and conversion design (mandatory gating before synthesis scale-up)
0.1 Acquire/solve the activated NUS-1a structure (from literature CIF if available; otherwise PXRD refinement) and build a periodic model.
0.2 Identify “braceable” phenyl-ring pairs: compute distributions of centroid–centroid distances and relative orientations between (i) dangling phenyl rings in the channel and (ii) phenyl rings on neighboring linkers within the first and second coordination shells. Use a simple protocol that is reproducible: (a) periodic DFTB/force-field optimization (UFF4MOF or MOF-FF) and (b) geometric screening for aryl–aryl coupling feasibility (distance window and dihedral accessibility).
0.3 Define a **design criterion** for crosslinker length: choose a linker that spans the modal candidate distance (d*) with tolerance ±0.3–0.5 Å after accounting for aryl–aryl bond formation geometry; generate 2–3 discrete crosslinkers (short/medium/long) around d*.
0.4 Predefine a **target conversion window** that preserves porosity: aim for 10–30% conversion of reactive handles at 5–10 mol% handle loading (net 0.5–3% of linkers crosslinked). Set acceptance criteria: (i) PXRD peak positions maintained (no phase change), (ii) Ar(87 K) BET retained ≥70% of pristine NUS-1a, and (iii) diffusion accessibility maintained (vapor uptake kinetics half-time within 2× pristine).

Step 1 — Baseline NUS-1/NUS-1a synthesis and a chloroform-free activation history (reference map)
1.1 Synthesize NUS-1 and activate to NUS-1a following the NUS-1a literature route but implement activation without chloroform (MeOH exchange → supercritical CO2 drying or gentle thermal activation under dynamic vacuum), to avoid solvent-history confounds.
1.2 Establish baseline structure–property metrics:
- Crystallinity/topology: PXRD + Le Bail/Rietveld check.
- Porosity: Ar 87 K isotherms; NLDFT/QSDFT pore size distribution (report differential PSD and uncertainty).
- Defects/composition: digestion 1H NMR (linker ratio), ICP-OES/MS (Zn), TGA.
- Photophysics: absolute quantum yield (integrating sphere), TCSPC lifetime, temperature-dependent PL (to parameterize knr(T)).
1.3 Baseline CHCl3 response: single-component CHCl3 vapor sorption (298 K) + in situ PL/QY vs partial pressure to define the unmodified turn-on curve and saturation regime.

Step 2 — Build reactive-handle NUS-1a variants with minimal topology perturbation
2.1 Mixed-linker strategy: prepare isoreticular NUS-1a containing 5, 10, and 15 mol% of a DPEB analogue bearing para-reactive handles positioned to project into the pore (two orthogonal handle sets for main + contingency routes):
- Set A (Suzuki/Ullmann option): para-bromo (or para-iodo) DPEB and complementary para-boronate DPEB (statistical incorporation; enables intrapore cross-coupling).
- Set B (click contingency): para-alkenyl (e.g., styrenyl) DPEB or para-azide/alkyne DPEB.
2.2 Confirm handle incorporation and preservation of NUS-1a structure: digestion 1H NMR (handle %), PXRD, Ar(87 K) sorption.

Step 3 — Intrapore bracing reaction with bounded, diffusion-controlled protocol + external-surface passivation
3.0 External-surface passivation (to suppress external polymerization/pore-mouth clogging): cap external reactive handles prior to coupling by brief exposure to a bulky, mono-functional “quench” reagent that cannot enter pores (size-exclusion chosen based on PSD; e.g., a bulky arylboronic acid or thiol with size > pore window), then wash thoroughly. Validate passivation by ToF-SIMS depth profiling (surface-enriched signal only).

3.1 Primary route (intrapore Suzuki–Miyaura bracing; only if stability gates are met)
- Crosslinker: geometry-selected di-boronate or di-halo aryl (from Step 0: short/medium/long around d*).
- Catalyst system: Pd(dppf)Cl2 (or Pd(PPh3)4) at ≤0.5–1 mol% relative to reactive sites.
- Base/solvent: weak inorganic base (K2CO3 or Cs2CO3) with rigorously limited water activity; use EtOH/toluene with controlled micro-water (≤1–2 vol%) to enable base solubility but minimize Zn-carboxylate hydrolysis.
- Temperature/time: 50–70 °C, 2–12 h; run time-series aliquots to stop in the target conversion window.
- Reaction format: packed-bed flow-through or gentle agitation with crystal-size control to promote uniform diffusion; track conversion vs time.
- Post-reaction cleanup: iterative solvent exchange (EtOH/MeOH), chelator wash (EDTA in alcohol), then activation. Verify Pd removal by ICP-MS.

3.2 Contingency route (MOF-compatible click chemistry; pre-planned, not “if time permits”)
Option B1: Thiol–ene intrapore bracing
- Use DPEB-styrenyl handles + a dithiol crosslinker of geometry-selected length.
- Initiation: photoinitiated (365–405 nm) or thermal radical initiator at low loading under oxygen-controlled conditions.
- Advantages: no strong base/water; typically high-yield; mild to Zn4O-carboxylate.
Option B2: CuAAC intrapore bracing
- Use azide/alkyne handles + difunctional alkyne/azide linker.
- Cu(I) source: CuBr + ligand (TBTA) at low loading; rigorous chelation wash post-reaction; monitor Cu by ICP-MS.

Step 4 — Decisive chemical proof of *intrapore covalent bracing* and spatial uniformity (mandatory)
4.1 Digest-and-analyze coupled fragments:
- Fully digest MOF (acidic digestion appropriate to Zn-carboxylate) and analyze by LC–MS and 1H/13C NMR to detect crosslinked linker–linker or linker–crosslinker adducts (mass shifts diagnostic of specific coupling). Quantify adduct fraction to determine true crosslink conversion.
4.2 Isotopic labeling for unambiguous assignment:
- Use 13C-labeled crosslinker (or 2H-labeled) and confirm incorporation by solid-state 13C CP/MAS NMR (appearance of labeled resonances) and ToF-SIMS mapping (labeled fragment distribution).
4.3 Spatial uniformity across crystallites:
- Perform confocal Raman/fluorescence mapping (if handle has distinct tag) and/or ToF-SIMS depth profiling on microtomed crystals to verify intrapore distribution (core vs shell). Pair with size-selected crystal batches to quantify diffusion limitations.
4.4 Rule out “pore fouling/graphitization-like byproducts”:
- Compare digestion LC–MS/NMR signatures with those from deliberate external polymerization control (Step 5 controls) to ensure the observed products correspond to discrete covalent braces rather than oligomeric tar.

Step 5 — Orthogonal controls explicitly demanded by reviewers (pre-registered)
C1 Catalyst/thermal-history control: expose pristine NUS-1a (no handles) to identical catalyst/base/solvent/time; assess PXRD, BET, PL/QY to quantify catalyst-induced changes.
C2 Inert-aryl control: use a mono-functional aryl analogue (cannot crosslink) under identical conditions to test adsorption/PL changes from mere guest uptake or physisorbed aromatic species.
C3 External-only coupling control: pre-block pore entrances with a reversible bulky guest, then run coupling; if crosslinking signatures appear only at the surface (ToF-SIMS), it validates the diffusion selectivity assumptions.
C4 Surface-passivation control: run coupling with and without external passivation; compare BET/PSD and depth profiles to quantify external polymerization contribution.

Step 6 — Quantify PSD tightening, accessibility, and CHCl3 binding energetics (structure–adsorption linkage)
6.1 PSD/accessibility: Ar 87 K + NLDFT/QSDFT (differential PSD), PALS for sub-nm free-volume change, and vapor uptake kinetics (time constants) for CHCl3/DCM/toluene.
6.2 CHCl3 binding strength/residence proxies:
- CHCl3 vapor isotherms at multiple temperatures (e.g., 298/308/318 K) to extract isosteric heats (Clausius–Clapeyron).
- In situ DRIFTS and/or solid-state NMR with CDCl3 to identify binding environments and distinguish specific confinement vs nonspecific condensation.

Step 7 — Photophysics with causality separation (rigidification vs pore redistribution vs guest-assisted RIM)
7.1 Intrinsic rigidification (no guest): compare QY and lifetime of activated samples under inert atmosphere; compute kr and knr (QY + TCSPC).
7.2 Guest-assisted rigidification: measure in situ PL/QY vs CHCl3 partial pressure; fit a two-regime model (low-loading “binding-site” regime vs high-loading “pore-filling” regime) to separate occupancy-dependent effects.
7.3 Decouple uptake from RIM: introduce a size-mismatched non-emissive guest that occupies volume but does not enhance emission (or use an analyte with similar uptake but different turn-on) to test whether QY tracks uptake alone.
7.4 Temperature-dependent PL (guest-free and guest-loaded) to verify suppression of vibrationally assisted nonradiative decay after bracing (reduced knr(T) slope).

Step 8 — Competitive selectivity, humidity tolerance, and quantitative sensing metrics (pre-registered)
8.1 Competitive vapor mixtures (mandatory): perform dynamic breakthrough-style vapor exposure and/or gravimetric mixture sorption with CHCl3 competing against DCM, CCl4, and toluene (and optionally acetone) at controlled partial pressures. Collect simultaneous PL response.
8.2 Humidity studies: run CHCl3 sensing at defined RH (0%, 30%, 60%) to test water interference and framework robustness; measure any QY drift and PXRD after cycling.
8.3 Sensing metric definitions (pre-registered):
- LOD: 3σ/slope using replicate blank noise (n≥10) and linear region of calibration curve (define exposure time and equilibration criterion).
- Response time: t90 (time to reach 90% of steady-state PL intensity) under a defined flow rate and film thickness/crystal mass.
- Reversibility: ≥20 adsorption/desorption cycles with maintained PXRD + BET retention ≥70% and PL baseline drift ≤10%.

Decision gates and success criteria (go/no-go)
G1 (post-crosslink): PXRD maintained + BET ≥70% + definitive digest-MS evidence of covalent adducts.
G2 (mechanism): QY increase must be explained primarily by decreased knr (not only increased uptake), and must correlate with PSD narrowing metrics (NLDFT/PALS) and/or increased CHCl3 isosteric heat.
G3 (selectivity): mixture experiments must show statistically significant preferential CHCl3 PL turn-on vs DCM/CCl4/toluene at equal partial pressures; humidity tolerance demonstrated at ≥30% RH.

Deliverable library
- Pristine NUS-1a
- Handle-only mixed-linker NUS-1a (no crosslink)
- Crosslinked series (low/medium/high conversion within target window)
- Full set of controls (C1–C4)
- Contingency-click crosslinked analogues (if primary route fails gates)
Feasibility:
Chemoselectivity and framework integrity: The main feasibility risk (Pd/Cu coupling damaging Zn4O-carboxylate or causing uncontrolled polymerization) is addressed by (i) a geometry-constrained crosslinker choice derived from the actual NUS-1a pore geometry (reducing off-path coupling), (ii) a low-handle, low-conversion regime explicitly defined to preserve accessible porosity, (iii) diffusion-bounded protocols with crystal-size control and time-series stopping, and (iv) external-surface passivation to suppress surface-initiated oligomerization that would masquerade as “intrapore bracing.” Any catalyst/solvent/thermal effects are quantified via mandatory catalyst-exposure controls (C1).

Decisive proof of covalent intrapore bracing: Rather than relying on non-specific FTIR/Raman changes, the plan requires (a) digestion followed by LC–MS and NMR identification/quantification of the exact coupled adducts, and (b) isotopic labeling (13C/2H) with solid-state NMR and ToF-SIMS mapping to verify incorporation and spatial distribution (core vs shell), directly addressing reviewer concerns about distinguishing true bracing from pore fouling.

Causality separation: The hypothesis explicitly distinguishes intrinsic rigidification, PSD redistribution, and guest-assisted RIM, and the execution plan separates them experimentally by guest-free photophysics (intrinsic effect), PSD/uptake measurements (pore effect), and controlled loading/temperature dependence plus decoupling controls (guest-assisted effect vs mere uptake). Extracting kr/knr from QY+TCSPC provides the required mechanistic discriminator.

Selectivity claims made testable: Competitive mixture experiments (CHCl3 vs DCM/CCl4/toluene) and humidity-defined protocols are built into the core plan with pre-registered LOD and response-time definitions, preventing over-attribution to PSD changes alone.

Contingency chemistry: If Suzuki/Ullmann compromises crystallinity or porosity, the proposal contains a pre-engineered click-chemistry branch (thiol–ene or CuAAC) using built-in handles designed at the mixed-linker stage, enabling intrapore bracing under milder, MOF-compatible conditions that avoid strong base/high water activity. This maintains the central concept chain (intrapore covalent bracing → RIM/PSD control → enhanced CHCl3 turn-on QY) while reducing synthetic risk.
Critique:
Methodological resolution is strong: the plan contains gated decision criteria, orthogonal controls for catalyst/thermal history and surface fouling, and a rare level of rigor in proving covalent intrapore bracing (digest-MS + isotopic labeling + depth profiling). The mechanistic chain (brace → higher torsional barriers → lower knr; brace → PSD tightening → higher CHCl3 residence/occupancy; guest-assisted RIM separated by loading/temperature) is logically coherent and experimentally testable.

Primary deductions are feasibility and interpretability risks that remain under-addressed at a quantitative level. (i) Intrapore aryl–aryl cross-coupling in Zn4O-carboxylate MOFs is still high-risk: even “mild” carbonate base with trace water and Pd can induce node hydrolysis/defect formation or linker exchange; the proposal includes controls but not a quantitative stability model (rates/thresholds) or a hard backstop if partial amorphization preserves PXRD but changes defect density that itself alters PL. (ii) “PSD narrowing/homogenization” at 0.5–3% crosslinked linkers may be too subtle to robustly resolve by NLDFT/QSDFT on Ar(87 K) alone; model-dependence and uncertainty could dominate the claimed effect size, and PALS sensitivity/interpretation in flexible/defective MOFs is nontrivial. (iii) The assumption that CHCl3 selectivity will materially increase via aperture redistribution is plausible but not yet anchored to predicted adsorption selectivity (e.g., IAST/GCMC or Henry constants) versus competing guests with similar kinetic diameters/polarizabilities (DCM/CCl4), so the selectivity gate may fail even if bracing succeeds. (iv) Photophysics causality: extracting kr/knr from QY+TCSPC is correct, but heterogeneous emissive populations (defects, partially crosslinked domains, surface vs core) can make single-/bi-exponential lifetime fits ambiguous; without a predefined global analysis model, “knr decrease” could be over-claimed.

Hypothesis: A plasmon-active, facet-programmed Zr6-oxo SURMOF can deliver **substrate-level photocatalytic selectivity** under visible light *without polymer imprinting* if—and only if—the **entire catalytically competent volume is confined to the verified plasmonic interaction zone (≤20–40 nm from Au nanorod hot spots)** and if the **rate-determining step is inner-sphere electron transfer (ET) that is distance/orientation gated by framework-encoded recognition linkers**. The revised mechanism explicitly resolves the reviewer’s length-scale concern by redesigning the architecture so that (i) Au nanorods (AuNRs) are **partially embedded** within the top layers of an ultrathin, oriented SURMOF (total thickness 20–35 nm), and (ii) node-anchored In(III)-chalcogen/oxide acceptor motifs are **localized to the same top region** (0–20 nm depth) via defect-directed installation, ensuring that all productive ET events occur within the LSPR near-field/hot-carrier reach. Mechanistically, on-resonance LSPR drives selectivity via two falsifiable contributions that are separated by controls: (1) **field-enhanced interfacial charge-transfer (PICT/LMCT-like) at bound complexes**—only guests that form a specific coordination/H-bonding complex at recognition linkers achieve the short tunneling distance and defined orbital alignment needed for fast inner-sphere ET; (2) **hot-carrier injection from Au into In–S/In–O acceptor states** (or into a linker/guest acceptor state that is electronically coupled to In clusters), which increases the population of reactive electrons at the bound complex. Nonbinding analogues remain outer-sphere/weakly adsorbed, where ET is slower and becomes kinetically suppressed. The gating claim is made falsifiable by (a) enforcing geometric confinement (all sites within 20–35 nm), (b) measuring energetic alignment (UPS/APS + spectroelectrochemistry), (c) implementing a **dielectric-spacer thickness series** that yields an exponential distance dependence (extract β) expected for ET but not for adsorption, and (d) imposing stringent photothermal/equal-absorption controls to exclude heating-driven selectivity.
Plan:
Step 1 — Architecture redesign around the plasmonic interaction volume (mandatory near-field coherence)
1.1 Ultrafilm SURMOF with single-facet exposure: Select a Zr6 MOF that is (i) water-stable, (ii) supports oriented SURMOF growth, and (iii) tolerates mixed-linker substitution. Primary choice: UiO-67-derived SURMOF (bpdc family) on FTO/ITO with (111)-preferred orientation. Grow by liquid-phase epitaxy (LPE) with a fixed cycle protocol to target **20–35 nm** thickness (not 80–150 nm): e.g., 15–25 deposition cycles, calibrated by ellipsometry/QCM-D. Terminate with a Zr-rich surface (node-terminated) to maximize phosphonate anchoring density.
1.2 Confining catalysis to the top reaction zone: Install In acceptor motifs only in the top portion of the film by **post-growth, diffusion-limited infiltration** (short contact time; low solvent swelling) and/or by a **two-layer SURMOF stack**: bottom 10–15 nm “inert” UiO-67 (no defects, no In), top 10–20 nm “active” UiO-67 (defect-enriched + In-installation). Defects tuned via modulator: formic acid/acetic acid ratio and controlled missing-linker fraction (target 3–8% missing-linker) to create μ3–OH/μ3–O defect sites for In binding.

Step 2 — Embed AuNRs into the MOF instead of placing them above it (mandatory length-scale fix)
2.1 Deterministic AuNR metasurface fabrication (geometry-controlled hot spots): Fabricate an ordered AuNR array on a sacrificial stamp by NIL/e-beam. Target dimensions: length 70 ± 10 nm; diameter 20–25 nm; pitch 120–200 nm (to avoid strong far-field coupling that broadens resonances uncontrollably). Tune longitudinal LSPR to 650–750 nm in water.
2.2 Transfer and partial embedding into SURMOF: Transfer-print AuNRs onto the *half-grown* SURMOF (e.g., after 8–12 LPE cycles, ~10–15 nm thickness). Then continue LPE growth (“growth-over”) for an additional 10–15 nm to **partially embed rods** so the rod sidewalls/tips reside within or immediately adjacent to MOF porosity. Outcome: essentially all active sites (recognition linkers + In motifs) are within ≤20–40 nm of Au hot spots.
2.3 Verify embedding and pore accessibility: Cross-sectional TEM/SEM (FIB lamella), GISAXS/GIWAXS (order/orientation), and dye-uptake/QCM-D to confirm that growth-over does not seal pores.

Step 3 — Replace speculative ALD windows with a concrete, distance-series dielectric spacer strategy (mandatory)
3.1 Uniform ultrathin dielectric spacer on AuNRs (no patterning/windows): Coat AuNR array *before* growth-over with **conformal Al2O3 by low-temperature ALD** (≤80–100 °C) at precisely controlled thickness t = 0.0, 0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 nm (series). This is a literature-standard strategy to (i) prevent Au corrosion/ligand loss in water, (ii) suppress indiscriminate charge recombination at metal surfaces, and (iii) create a tunable tunneling barrier.
3.2 Define the falsifiable ET-distance experiment: For each t(Al2O3), hold AuNR geometry, MOF thickness (20–35 nm), In loading, and guest coverage constant. Measure photocatalytic rate constants for target vs analogues. Expectation for ET gating: log(k) decreases approximately linearly with t (effective barrier thickness), yielding an apparent β; adsorption-only selectivity should not exhibit an exponential dependence on t.
3.3 Add an orthogonal molecular spacer series at the recognition linker: Introduce recognition linkers with systematically varied electronic coupling lengths (e.g., phenyl vs biphenyl vs terphenyl spacer between bpdc backbone and binding group) while keeping binding group identity constant. This provides a second, independent β extraction.

Step 4 — Interface recognition chemistry made explicit and robust in water
4.1 Framework-encoded recognition linkers (functional-monomer analogue): Mixed-linker UiO-67 with 5–12% functionalized bpdc derivatives. Two prioritized chemistries (chosen for aqueous robustness and defined coordination/H-bonding):
  (a) N-heteroaromatic chelation: bpdc-(CH2)n-pyridyl (n = 0–2) to promote fluoroquinolone binding via zwitterion/H-bond + metal-assisted coordination.
  (b) Directional H-bonding: bpdc-urea/sulfonamide substituents oriented into the pore aperture nearest the AuNR interface.
Synthesis: incorporate during LPE using mixed-linker precursor solutions; confirm composition by digestion NMR/LC-MS of linkers and XPS on films.
4.2 Minimal, stable Au–MOF coupling chemistry compatible with Al2O3 spacer: Rather than relying on Au–thiol directly (blocked by Al2O3), couple the MOF growth-over and interface proximity as the primary “attachment.” Any chemical anchoring is implemented at the MOF side: phosphonate groups bind Zr6 nodes to position recognition motifs; the dielectric spacer ensures defined separation without requiring reactive windows.

Step 5 — In–S/In–O acceptor-state engineering with energetic justification and recombination controls
5.1 Node-directed In installation localized to the top zone: Expose the finished embedded architecture to In(NO3)3 in ethanol/water (low swelling) for short times (e.g., 5–30 min) to limit penetration depth. Rinse thoroughly.
5.2 Controlled conversion to In–S/In–O motifs: Convert with thioacetamide at ≤70–80 °C (aqueous/ethanolic) to generate ultrasmall In–S clusters; optionally mild air/hydrolysis to introduce In–O/In–S mixed motifs. Avoid large nanoparticles by limiting precursor concentration and time; confirm with XPS (In 3d, S 2p), EXAFS (In–S/In–O coordination), and TEM (absence of >2–3 nm particles).
5.3 Recombination/trap-state controls: Prepare matched films with (i) In installed but not sulfided (In–O dominant), (ii) sulfided without AuNRs, (iii) AuNRs without In, (iv) neither. These decouple “trap-mediated recombination” vs “acceptor-mediated charge separation.”

Step 6 — Explicit energy-level scheme + measurements (mandatory)
6.1 Define the energy-level hypothesis quantitatively: Measure/compile (a) Au Fermi level/work function (ΦAu) and its shift with Al2O3 and environment; (b) MOF valence/conduction proxy levels (linker-based states) and defect states; (c) In–S/In–O acceptor levels; (d) guest redox potentials (E1/2) for target and analogues. Predict whether hot-electron injection Au→In or Au→(guest/linker) is thermodynamically plausible under illumination.
6.2 Measurements on the actual films: UPS (work function, valence onset), ambient photoemission/APS (electron affinity trend), and in situ spectroelectrochemistry (UV–Vis under applied potential) to map polaron/charge-transfer signatures. Use Mott–Schottky/EIS cautiously (MOFs are not classical semiconductors) but employ them comparatively across controls.

Step 7 — Reaction selection and selectivity metric designed for inner-sphere ET discrimination
7.1 Model transformation: Visible-light reductive dehalogenation of a halogenated fluoroquinolone (target) versus non-halogenated or differently substituted analogues (controls), or selective oxidation of ciprofloxacin vs norfloxacin/ofloxacin where binding modes differ subtly.
7.2 Quantification: LC-MS/MS for substrate depletion and product distribution; define selectivity as (kapp,target/kapp,analogue) at equal surface coverage.
7.3 Equal-coverage protocol (mandatory adsorption control): Pre-adsorb each substrate to identical θ (measured by depletion/HPLC) prior to illumination; run kinetics under identical photon flux.

Step 8 — Discriminant mechanistic tests tying observables to inner-sphere vs outer-sphere ET (mandatory strengthening)
8.1 Distance-series ET signature: For Al2O3 thickness series, fit ln(kapp) vs t to extract β; require that target shows a different β/intercept consistent with stronger electronic coupling due to binding geometry.
8.2 Dark electrochemical ET test (mandatory): Using the FTO/SURMOF electrode, perform dark electrochemical reduction/oxidation of bound substrates at controlled potentials (no light). If binding enforces inner-sphere ET, target should show lower overpotential/faster heterogeneous ET than analogues at equal θ. This directly links “recognition” to ET kinetics independent of plasmonics.
8.3 Hot-carrier vs field-only separation: Compare (i) AuNR on-resonance excitation, (ii) off-resonance excitation with equal absorbed power, (iii) a nonplasmonic metal control (e.g., Pd nanorods with damped LSPR in visible or Au spheres tuned away from excitation), and (iv) dielectric-only nanorod replica (no metal) to isolate pure photothermal.
8.4 Photothermal calibration (mandatory): Measure local/average temperature rises via (a) embedded fluorescent thermometry dye in a sacrificial analog film or (b) Raman thermometry on the substrate; then perform heating-matched dark reactions and off-resonance heating-matched illuminated runs. Selectivity must persist after matching temperature profiles.
8.5 Reactive-species controls (secondary): Scavengers (EDTA, benzoquinone, isopropanol) and isotope labeling where relevant; interpret only after the ET-distance and energy-alignment tests.

Step 9 — Stability and leaching under realistic matrices
9.1 Cycle tests in buffered water + NOM + common ions; monitor LSPR peak stability (UV–Vis–NIR), GIWAXS for MOF integrity, and ICP-MS for Au/In leaching.
9.2 Fouling tolerance: Compare performance before/after exposure to humic substances; quantify any loss of recognition binding constants (adsorption isotherms) and correlate with selectivity changes.

Milestones / Go–No-Go criteria
M1 (architecture): Demonstrate MOF thickness 20–35 nm; AuNR partial embedding confirmed by cross-sectional TEM; retained porosity/uptake.
M2 (energetics): UPS/APS + spectroelectrochemistry show feasible alignment for hot-electron injection and/or field-enhanced interfacial CT.
M3 (falsifiable gating): Exponential distance dependence of kapp on Al2O3 thickness and/or linker spacer length; selectivity persists at equal θ and under heating-matched controls.
M4 (mechanistic linkage): Dark electrochemical ET discriminates target vs analogue in a manner consistent with the photocatalytic selectivity trend.
Feasibility:
Addresses (1) length-scale/field mismatch: The revised design eliminates the 80–150 nm film assumption and instead **forces all catalytically relevant chemistry into a 20–35 nm SURMOF** with **AuNR partial embedding** via growth-over. This directly implements the reviewer’s directive so the plasmonic near-field/hot-carrier flux overlaps essentially the full active zone; the gating claim no longer depends on framework-wide penetration of |E|2.

Addresses (2) under-specified interface chemistry / ALD windows: The proposal removes the speculative “windowed ALD” concept and replaces it with a **uniform, thickness-controlled Al2O3 spacer series** (0–2 nm) that is actionable, reproducible, and intrinsically quantitative. Because rods are embedded by MOF overgrowth, mechanical/chemical stability is achieved without relying on fragile Au–thiol linkages in water, while the dielectric spacer provides a defined tunneling barrier and corrosion protection.

Addresses (3) energetic alignment + discriminant tests: A **measured energy-level scheme** (UPS/APS + spectroelectrochemistry + guest redox potentials) is now central, enabling a justified claim for hot-carrier injection versus field-only enhancement. Potential trap/recombination risks from In–S/In–O are treated as a design variable with explicit controls (In-only, Au-only, neither) and localized installation to avoid bulk trapping. Mechanistic attribution is made falsifiable through (i) distance-series β extraction (ET hallmark), (ii) equal-coverage kinetics to eliminate adsorption artifacts, (iii) dark electrochemical ET to directly test inner-sphere ET advantages conferred by recognition linkers, and (iv) stringent photothermal controls with absorbed-power matching and heating-matched experiments.

Grounding in provided assets: Asset 1 motivates the importance of metal/semiconductor junctions and internal fields for charge transport; here AuNR LSPR provides resonant carrier generation/fields while In motifs serve as acceptors. Asset 2 supports the heterojunction principle that In-based components improve visible-light photocatalysis via charge separation; here the In acceptors are node-anchored and spatially confined to the plasmonically addressable zone. Asset 3 validates that “functional monomer” chemistry on MOF scaffolds can generate selectivity; here that logic is translated into **mixed-linker, framework-encoded recognition** that gates ET rather than relying on an imprinted polymer shell.

Overall, the refined proposal is technically ambitious but now architecturally consistent with plasmonic length scales, chemically concrete at the interface, and experimentally designed so the selectivity-by-ET-gating claim can be disproven (or supported) by clear, quantitative signatures.
Critique: The redesign directly addresses the prior length-scale mismatch and replaces the previously speculative ‘windowed ALD’ with a reproducible spacer-series experiment, which is a major engineering upgrade. The mechanistic claim (inner-sphere ET gating by recognition linkers within the plasmonic zone) is largely coherent and appropriately falsifiable via (i) Al2O3 thickness dependence, (ii) linker electronic-length series, and (iii) dark heterogeneous ET metrics at equal coverage. Score deductions stem from several remaining high-risk or under-specified points: (1) Partial embedding + subsequent LPE growth over ALD-coated AuNRs can disrupt SURMOF orientation, introduce voids, or seal transport pathways; the proposal lists characterization but not contingency process windows (surface chemistry, nucleation strategy on Al2O3, defect control while maintaining crystallinity). (2) The interpretation of an exponential ln(k)–t(Al2O3) dependence is not uniquely diagnostic of inner-sphere ET in this geometry: t also perturbs local field amplitude at the reaction zone and changes interfacial capacitance/ion distribution; without independent near-field mapping or a field-only control that preserves ET coupling, β extraction may be confounded. (3) The In–S/In–O ‘acceptor’ role risks becoming a variable density of midgap traps that alter selectivity via differential radical pathways rather than distance/orientation-gated ET; EXAFS/XPS/TEM help, but the plan lacks operando identification of the actual reduced intermediate(s) and a kinetic model separating injection, hopping/transport in the MOF, and substrate ET. (4) The ‘equal coverage’ requirement is good but practically challenging in thin SURMOFs with competitive binding and possible photodesorption; selectivity could still reflect different residence times or diffusion limitations rather than ET kinetics unless residence-time/diffusion are measured. Overall: technically ambitious, substantially improved in rigor, but still vulnerable to alternative explanations unless the field-vs-ET and transport-vs-ET separations are strengthened.
